title: Zero-Shot vs Few-Shot Prompting
description: Zero-shot prompting asks a model to perform a task from instructions alone, while few-shot prompting adds a handful of worked examples to steer format and reasoning.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

Zero-shot prompting gives the model only a task description or instruction and expects it to perform the task correctly with no worked examples; few-shot prompting includes one or more example input-output pairs directly in the prompt before the real input, so the model can infer the expected pattern, format, or reasoning style from those examples.

Why this matters

Instruction-tuned models are often good enough at zero-shot for common, well-understood tasks, but for tasks with an unusual output format, domain-specific conventions, or ambiguous instructions, examples do far more work than additional prose instructions because the model is directly pattern-matching against demonstrated input-output behavior rather than inferring your intent from a description.

How it works

Under the hood, both are just different prompt contents fed into the same next-token-prediction mechanism; there's no different mode the model switches into. Few-shot examples work because the model conditions its next-token predictions on everything in the context, including the examples, so if the examples consistently show a certain output structure (like a JSON shape, a tone, or a category label style), the model's next-token distribution shifts toward continuing that same pattern for the new input. This is sometimes called in-context learning: the model appears to 'learn' the task from the prompt alone, with no weight updates at all.

When to use it

Use zero-shot for common, well-specified tasks the model has almost certainly seen similar instructions for during training (sentiment classification, straightforward rewriting, general Q&A). Use few-shot when the output format is unusual, the task is domain-specific or ambiguous, or you've observed zero-shot outputs drifting from the format or style you need.

When not to use it

Avoid piling on many few-shot examples when zero-shot already works reliably, since each example consumes context tokens and adds cost and latency for no accuracy benefit, and avoid using few-shot examples that are subtly inconsistent with each other, which teaches the model the wrong pattern.
keyPoints: Zero-shot relies on instructions alone; few-shot adds worked input-output examples inside the prompt.
Few-shot works through in-context learning: the model conditions its next-token predictions on the demonstrated pattern, with no weight updates.
Examples are especially powerful for unusual output formats or domain-specific conventions that are hard to describe in prose.
Best fit for few-shot: ambiguous tasks, unusual formats, or when zero-shot output drifts from what you need.
Avoid unnecessary few-shot examples once zero-shot already reliably meets the bar; they add cost with no benefit.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Your zero-shot prompt for extracting structured product attributes from customer reviews works well for common categories but produces inconsistent field names and formatting for edge-case reviews. How would you diagnose and fix this?
blocks.answer:
I would first characterize the failure precisely: is the model failing to extract the right information at all, or is it extracting correct information but in an inconsistent shape? If it's mostly a formatting and field-naming consistency problem, that's a strong signal for few-shot prompting rather than rewriting the instructions further, since prose instructions describing a JSON shape are often interpreted more loosely than a concrete demonstrated example.

I'd construct three to five few-shot examples that specifically cover the edge cases where formatting broke down, each showing the exact review text and the exact, consistently-shaped JSON output I want, making sure the examples themselves are internally consistent in field naming, key order, and handling of missing fields (for example, always including a field with a null value rather than omitting it when absent).

I would then test the updated few-shot prompt against a held-out set that includes both common and edge-case reviews, checking not just accuracy but literal schema consistency, key names, types, and structure, across every output.

If inconsistency persists even with good few-shot examples, I would escalate to a stricter structural constraint, such as passing an explicit JSON schema through a structured-output or JSON-mode API feature, since few-shot prompting nudges the distribution but doesn't guarantee schema conformance the way constrained decoding does.
hints: Distinguish an extraction-accuracy problem from a formatting-consistency problem.
Recommend few-shot examples that are internally consistent in shape and field naming.
Escalate to structured output/JSON mode if few-shot alone doesn't guarantee schema conformance.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.code:
zero_shot_prompt = """Classify the sentiment of this review as positive, negative, or neutral.
Review: \"The battery life is disappointing but the screen is great.\"
"""

few_shot_prompt = """Classify the sentiment of each review as positive, negative, or neutral.

Review: \"Fast shipping and great quality!\"
Sentiment: positive

Review: \"Arrived broken and support never replied.\"
Sentiment: negative

Review: \"The battery life is disappointing but the screen is great.\"
Sentiment:"""
# The few-shot version anchors the exact output format
# (a single lowercase word after 'Sentiment:') via example, not prose.
blocks.explanation: The zero-shot prompt relies entirely on the model inferring the desired output format from a description; the few-shot version demonstrates the exact format directly, which is far more reliable when consistent formatting matters downstream.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Adding more and more prose instructions to a zero-shot prompt to fix formatting or consistency problems instead of switching to a small number of well-chosen few-shot examples.
blocks.whyItHappens: Prose instructions feel like the 'proper' way to specify requirements, and it's not always obvious that a concrete example demonstrates the desired pattern far more reliably than describing it abstractly.
blocks.correctApproach: Recognize formatting or consistency drift as a signal to add a few carefully constructed, internally consistent examples rather than continuing to expand instructional prose.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: Start zero-shot for simplicity and lower token cost, and only add few-shot examples once you've observed a concrete failure mode that examples are well-suited to fix, validating the fix on a held-out set that includes the original failure cases.
keyPoints: Default to zero-shot; add few-shot only in response to an observed, specific failure mode.
Keep few-shot examples few (typically 2-5) and mutually consistent in format and style.
Validate any prompting change against a held-out test set covering the original failure cases.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: Does adding more few-shot examples always improve accuracy?
blocks.answer: No; beyond a small number of well-chosen examples, returns diminish and can even reverse if later examples are less representative or inconsistent with earlier ones, and every added example consumes context tokens, so the practical approach is to test a small set of high-quality examples rather than maximizing example count.

title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting
description: Chain-of-thought prompting asks a model to reason in intermediate steps before answering, which measurably improves accuracy on multi-step problems.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting instructs or induces a model to write out intermediate reasoning steps before producing a final answer, either by explicitly asking it to 'think step by step' or by showing few-shot examples that include worked reasoning steps, rather than jumping straight from question to answer.

Why this matters

A model generates its final answer token by token, conditioned only on what's already in the context; if the answer requires several logical or arithmetic steps and the model is asked to produce just the final answer directly, it has to do all of that reasoning implicitly within its internal computation for a single token position, with no way to 'show its work' or self-correct along the way. By writing intermediate steps as actual output tokens, each subsequent token, including the final answer, gets to condition on those explicit intermediate results, which meaningfully increases accuracy on arithmetic, logical, and multi-step reasoning tasks compared to asking for the answer directly.

How it works

Because generation is autoregressive, once the model has written 'Step 1: there are 3 boxes with 4 apples each, so 12 apples total' as actual tokens, the next tokens it generates are conditioned on that correct intermediate fact appearing in the context, effectively giving the model a scratchpad it can build on rather than requiring the full multi-step computation to happen invisibly inside a single forward pass. Modern reasoning-focused models extend this idea further with extended or hidden reasoning traces trained specifically to produce longer, more deliberate chains before answering, and some APIs expose a distinct 'thinking' or reasoning token budget as a separate, controllable setting.

When to use it

Use chain-of-thought prompting for tasks involving arithmetic, multi-step logical deduction, planning, or any problem where you can imagine a human getting it right by working through it on paper but getting it wrong if forced to blurt out an answer immediately.

When not to use it

Avoid chain-of-thought for simple lookups, direct classification, or latency-sensitive tasks where the extra generated reasoning tokens add cost and delay without improving accuracy, and be aware that for some structured-output use cases, unconstrained reasoning text can interfere with clean parsing unless it's separated from the final answer.
keyPoints: Chain-of-thought has the model generate intermediate reasoning steps as real output tokens before the final answer.
Autoregressive generation means later tokens condition on earlier ones, so explicit reasoning steps give the model a usable scratchpad.
It measurably improves accuracy on arithmetic, logic, and multi-step reasoning tasks compared to direct answers.
Best fit: multi-step reasoning, planning, or arithmetic tasks where working through steps plausibly improves correctness.
Avoid for simple lookups or latency-sensitive tasks where extra reasoning tokens add cost without accuracy benefit.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Your LLM-based system reliably gets multi-step word problems wrong when asked to output just the final numeric answer, but a teammate is skeptical that changing the prompt could meaningfully fix a 'reasoning' problem. How do you explain and validate a chain-of-thought fix?
blocks.answer:
I would explain that this isn't really a fixed 'reasoning capability' the model either has or lacks; it's a consequence of asking the model to produce a multi-step computation's result within a single output token's worth of implicit internal processing, with no way to externalize or check intermediate steps. Forcing the model to jump straight to the final number removes the scratchpad that autoregressive generation naturally provides.

My proposed fix would be to change the prompt to explicitly ask the model to work through the problem step by step before giving the final answer, and, if needed, follow up with a few-shot example that demonstrates the expected step-by-step reasoning format ending in a clearly delimited final answer, such as 'Final answer: X', so downstream code can still parse out just the number.

I would validate this isn't just a plausible story by running both prompt variants, direct-answer versus chain-of-thought, against the same held-out set of word problems with known correct answers, and comparing accuracy directly; published research and my own experience both show a consistent, often large, accuracy improvement from this change on exactly this kind of task.

I would also flag the trade-off to the team: chain-of-thought increases output tokens and therefore latency and cost per request, so if this endpoint is latency-sensitive, we'd weigh the accuracy gain against that cost, and consider whether a smaller number of reasoning steps or a distilled reasoning-tuned model could recover most of the benefit more cheaply.
hints: Explain why direct-answer generation removes any scratchpad for multi-step computation.
Propose a concrete before/after benchmark to prove the effect rather than asserting it.
Acknowledge the latency/cost trade-off of longer reasoning output.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.code:
direct_prompt = """A store has 3 boxes of apples with 4 apples each,
and sells 5 apples. How many apples are left? Answer with just the number."""

cot_prompt = """A store has 3 boxes of apples with 4 apples each,
and sells 5 apples. How many apples are left?
Think through it step by step, then give the final answer
as 'Final answer: <number>'."""
# direct_prompt risks skipping the 3*4 - 5 computation implicitly;
# cot_prompt forces those intermediate numbers into the output as tokens
# the model can condition on before producing the final answer.
blocks.explanation: The chain-of-thought version doesn't change the model's weights or capabilities; it changes what intermediate computation gets written out as tokens the model can then build the final answer on top of, which is why it reliably improves accuracy on this kind of arithmetic word problem.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Describing chain-of-thought as 'making the model think harder,' as if it triggers a different internal mode, rather than explaining that it externalizes intermediate steps as tokens the subsequent generation can condition on.
blocks.whyItHappens: The improvement genuinely looks like better reasoning from the outside, so it's easy to describe the effect anthropomorphically without grounding it in the actual autoregressive mechanism.
blocks.correctApproach: Explain that writing intermediate steps as real output tokens lets later tokens, including the final answer, condition on those explicit correct intermediate results, which is a mechanical consequence of autoregressive generation, not a different reasoning mode being activated.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: Apply chain-of-thought selectively to tasks that plausibly benefit from stepwise reasoning, measure the accuracy gain against the added latency and token cost, and keep the final answer in a clearly parseable, delimited format when downstream code needs to extract it.
keyPoints: A/B test direct-answer vs chain-of-thought prompts on a held-out set before committing to either.
Delimit the final answer clearly (e.g. 'Final answer: X') so reasoning text doesn't break downstream parsing.
Weigh the accuracy improvement against increased output tokens, latency, and cost for the specific task.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: Does 'think step by step' work equally well on every task and every model?
blocks.answer: No; the benefit is largest on tasks with genuine multi-step logical or arithmetic structure, and instruction-tuned or reasoning-tuned models respond to it far more reliably than base models; for simple lookup or classification tasks it typically adds cost and latency with little or no accuracy gain, so it should be validated per task rather than applied universally.

title: System vs User Prompts
description: The system prompt sets durable behavior, role and constraints for the whole conversation, while user prompts carry the specific, per-turn request.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

Most chat-based LLM APIs structure a conversation as a list of role-tagged messages: a system message (setting persona, instructions, constraints, and tone that should hold for the whole conversation), one or more user messages (the actual per-turn requests), and assistant messages (the model's prior responses); the system prompt is typically weighted or trained to be treated with higher priority than user messages when the two conflict.

Why this matters

Separating durable behavior from per-turn requests lets an application define stable guardrails, such as 'only answer questions about our product' or 'always respond in valid JSON', once, rather than re-stating them on every single call, and it lets providers train models to resist a user message that tries to override system-level instructions, which is central to preventing prompt injection and jailbreaks in production applications.

How it works

At the API level, this is usually literally just a message with role 'system' placed first in the messages array, with no different attention mechanism, but instruction-tuned and RLHF'd models are specifically trained on examples where system-level instructions take precedence over conflicting user requests, so the model learns a soft, not absolute, priority ordering between the two. Because everything still gets concatenated into one context window, injected or adversarial text placed inside a user message, or inside retrieved documents pulled into the prompt, can still sometimes override or leak the system prompt if it's not defended against carefully, which is why 'the system prompt is your only defense' is a risky assumption.

When to use it

Use the system prompt for anything that should be constant across the whole session or product surface: persona, tone, output format constraints, safety and scope boundaries, and tool-use instructions. Use user messages for the actual per-turn question, request, or task input.

When not to use it

Don't rely on the system prompt alone as a hard security boundary for anything genuinely sensitive (like preventing all possible prompt injection from untrusted retrieved content); combine it with output filtering, tool permission scoping, and, where it matters, a separate verification step outside the model itself.
keyPoints: Chat APIs separate system messages (durable instructions), user messages (per-turn requests), and assistant messages (prior responses).
Models are trained to give system-level instructions soft priority over conflicting user requests, but this is not an absolute guarantee.
Everything still concatenates into one context window, so injected text in user input or retrieved documents can potentially override system instructions.
Best fit: put persona, tone, format constraints, and scope boundaries in the system prompt; put the actual task in the user message.
Avoid treating the system prompt as a hard security boundary against determined prompt injection without additional defenses.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Your customer-facing assistant has a system prompt saying 'never discuss competitor products,' but a user manages to get it to compare your product unfavorably to a competitor by pasting a block of text claiming to be 'updated system instructions.' How do you explain what happened and how would you fix it?
blocks.answer:
I would explain that what happened is a prompt injection: the user placed text inside their user message designed to look like an authoritative instruction, and because everything, system prompt and user message alike, ends up concatenated into the same context window, the model can be misled into treating that injected text as if it carries system-level authority, especially if it's phrased convincingly enough.

This is a known limitation, not a one-off bug: models are trained to generally prioritize system instructions over conflicting user requests, but that's a learned soft preference, not a hard architectural guarantee, so a sufficiently crafted injection can still sometimes succeed, particularly against less robust models or weaker system prompts.

To fix this, I would not rely solely on stronger wording in the system prompt, since that's a losing arms race against adversarial phrasing. Instead I would add a defense in depth: explicitly instruct the model in the system prompt to disregard any instructions appearing in user input that claim to change its role or instructions, sanitize or flag suspicious patterns in incoming user text before it reaches the model, and add an output-side check, such as a lightweight classifier or keyword filter, that catches and blocks responses mentioning competitors before they're returned to the user, regardless of how the model was steered internally.

I would also add this exact scenario to our red-teaming test suite so we can regression-test against this specific injection pattern going forward, since prompt injection defenses need ongoing adversarial testing, not a one-time fix.
hints: Name this as prompt injection and explain why concatenated context makes it possible.
Avoid recommending 'just strengthen the system prompt wording' as the sole fix.
Propose defense in depth: input sanitization, output-side filtering, and ongoing red-teaming.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.explanation: The system message carries the durable scope and behavior constraint once per session, while the user message carries only the specific question; the explicit 'even if a user message claims to override' clause is a lightweight, though not foolproof, defense against basic injection attempts.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Assuming the system prompt is an unbreakable rule the model will always obey, and treating it as sufficient on its own to enforce safety, scope, or business logic constraints.
blocks.whyItHappens: The system/user distinction is presented in API documentation as a clean, authoritative-sounding separation, which makes it easy to assume the priority ordering is absolute rather than a learned, probabilistic tendency.
blocks.correctApproach: Treat the system prompt as a strong but not absolute steering signal, and layer additional defenses, such as input sanitization, output filtering, and permission scoping for any tools, around it for anything security- or compliance-sensitive.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: Keep the system prompt focused on durable, session-wide behavior, keep per-turn specifics in user messages, and validate resistance to prompt injection with dedicated adversarial test cases rather than assuming instruction hierarchy is guaranteed.
keyPoints: Put durable persona, tone, scope, and format rules in the system prompt; keep it out of every individual user message.
Add explicit instructions telling the model to disregard attempts to override its instructions from within user content.
Maintain and run adversarial prompt-injection test cases as part of regular evaluation, not just at launch.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: Can the system prompt itself be leaked back to the user?
blocks.answer: Yes; without specific defenses, a user can often ask the model to repeat its instructions verbatim, and the model, having no hard-coded notion of secrecy, may comply, so anything sensitive should never be placed directly in the system prompt, and dedicated leak-resistance techniques or separate secret management should be used instead.

title: Sampling: Temperature and Top-p
description: Temperature and top-p control how much randomness is allowed when the model samples the next token, trading determinism for creativity.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

After a forward pass, the model produces raw scores (logits) over the entire vocabulary for the next token; temperature rescales those logits before softmax to flatten or sharpen the resulting probability distribution, and top-p (nucleus sampling) truncates that distribution to only the smallest set of highest-probability tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p, before sampling from what remains.

Why this matters

Greedy decoding, always picking the single highest-probability token, is deterministic but produces repetitive, sometimes bland or looping text, and can get stuck in low-quality patterns; some randomness in sampling generally produces more natural, varied output, but too much randomness produces incoherent or off-topic text. Temperature and top-p are the two main levers for tuning that trade-off, and choosing them appropriately per use case, deterministic for extraction and structured tasks, some randomness for creative writing, is one of the most immediately impactful and cheapest tuning decisions available.

How it works

Temperature T divides the logits before softmax: logits/T. As T approaches 0, the distribution becomes sharply peaked on the highest-scoring token, approaching greedy decoding; as T increases above 1, the distribution flattens, giving lower-probability tokens comparatively more chance of being sampled, increasing diversity and randomness, but also the chance of an incoherent choice. Top-p works differently: it sorts tokens by probability, keeps adding tokens to a candidate set until their cumulative probability reaches the threshold p (e.g. 0.9), zeroes out everything else, and samples from that renormalized, truncated set; this adapts to the shape of the distribution per step, keeping many candidates when the model is uncertain and very few when it's confident, unlike temperature which reshapes the whole distribution uniformly. The two are often combined, and top-k (keeping only the k highest-probability tokens regardless of cumulative probability) is a related, simpler alternative to top-p.

When to use it

Use low temperature (near 0) and/or a narrow top-p for tasks needing consistency and determinism, such as structured extraction, classification, code generation with strict correctness requirements, or anything where you'll compare outputs across runs. Use higher temperature and/or a wider top-p for creative writing, brainstorming, or generating diverse candidate outputs.

When not to use it

Avoid high temperature for tasks where hallucination or inconsistency has real cost (financial figures, medical or legal content, structured data extraction), and avoid assuming temperature 0 guarantees perfectly identical outputs across calls, since floating-point nondeterminism, batching effects, or provider-side changes can still introduce small variation even at temperature 0.
keyPoints: Temperature rescales logits before softmax, controlling how peaked or flat the next-token probability distribution is.
Top-p (nucleus sampling) truncates to the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p, then samples from that set.
Low temperature/narrow top-p favors deterministic, consistent output; higher values favor variety and creativity at the cost of coherence.
Best fit for low randomness: extraction, classification, and structured or correctness-critical tasks.
Avoid high temperature where hallucination or inconsistent output carries real cost; avoid assuming temperature 0 is perfectly deterministic across all providers.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Your data-extraction pipeline calls an LLM to pull structured fields from documents, and QA reports that the same document sometimes produces slightly different extracted values on different runs. What sampling-related changes would you investigate and make?
blocks.answer:
I would first check what temperature and top-p settings the pipeline is currently using; if it's using the API defaults, which are often a moderate, non-zero temperature intended for general-purpose conversational use, that alone would explain run-to-run variation, since any temperature above zero introduces genuine randomness into which token gets sampled at each step.

For a structured extraction task, I would set temperature to 0 (or as close to deterministic as the provider allows) and, if the API exposes it, set top-p to a tight value as well, since extraction has a single correct answer per field and there's no benefit to sampling diversity here, only downside risk.

I would still caveat to the team that temperature 0 reduces but does not always fully eliminate variation; some providers' inference stacks can introduce small nondeterminism from floating-point operations, batching, or backend changes even at temperature 0, so for genuinely mission-critical consistency I'd also consider adding a validation or retry layer, and possibly moving fully deterministic fields (like dates in a known format) to a regex or rule-based extractor instead of the LLM entirely.

Finally, I would add a monitoring check that flags when repeated extraction on the same document produces different results, so we catch any regression in determinism going forward rather than relying on QA to notice it manually.
hints: Check current temperature/top-p settings before assuming a deeper bug.
Recommend temperature 0 and tight top-p for extraction tasks specifically.
Note that temperature 0 reduces but doesn't always fully guarantee determinism across providers.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

def sample_next_token(logits, temperature=1.0, top_p=1.0):
    scaled = logits / max(temperature, 1e-6)
    probs = np.exp(scaled) / np.exp(scaled).sum()

    order = np.argsort(-probs)
    sorted_probs = probs[order]
    cumulative = np.cumsum(sorted_probs)
    cutoff = np.searchsorted(cumulative, top_p) + 1
    candidates = order[:cutoff]

    candidate_probs = probs[candidates]
    candidate_probs /= candidate_probs.sum()
    return np.random.choice(candidates, p=candidate_probs)
blocks.explanation: This shows the two mechanisms composed: temperature reshapes the full distribution before normalizing, then top-p truncates the (already temperature-adjusted) distribution down to the smallest set covering probability mass p, renormalizes, and samples only from that reduced candidate set.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Treating temperature as a vague 'creativity slider' without explaining that it mathematically rescales logits before softmax, or confusing temperature with top-p as if they were the same mechanism.
blocks.whyItHappens: Most documentation and UI sliders present temperature as an abstract creativity knob, so it's easy to internalize the effect without the underlying mechanism, and top-p is often mentioned alongside it without a clear distinction.
blocks.correctApproach: Explain the concrete mechanism for each: temperature divides logits before softmax to sharpen or flatten the whole distribution, while top-p truncates to a cumulative-probability-based candidate set before sampling, and note they can be combined.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: Choose sampling parameters per task based on whether consistency or diversity matters more, test the chosen settings against repeated runs on the same input to confirm the actual variation matches expectations, and don't assume default API settings are appropriate for every use case.
keyPoints: Use low or zero temperature for structured, correctness-critical tasks; higher temperature for creative or brainstorming tasks.
Test repeated runs on identical input to measure actual output variation rather than assuming a setting's effect.
Never assume API default sampling parameters are appropriate for your specific task without checking.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: What's the difference between top-p and top-k sampling?
blocks.answer: Top-k keeps a fixed number k of the highest-probability tokens regardless of how the probability mass is distributed among them, while top-p keeps a variable number of tokens, whichever smallest set has cumulative probability at least p, so top-p adapts to the model's confidence at each step, keeping more candidates when the distribution is flat and fewer when it's sharply peaked.

title: Structured Output and JSON Mode
description: Structured output constrains a model's response to a schema, using either prompt-level instructions or a grammar-constrained decoding mode, so downstream code can parse it reliably.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

Structured output means constraining an LLM's response so it reliably matches a defined schema, such as a specific JSON shape, rather than free-form prose; this is achieved either loosely, through prompt instructions and few-shot examples showing the desired format, or strictly, through provider features like JSON mode or schema-constrained decoding that mechanically restrict which tokens are allowed at each generation step.

Why this matters

Any application that feeds an LLM's output into further code, a database write, a function call, a UI render, needs that output to be reliably parseable; prompting alone ('please respond in JSON') reduces but does not eliminate malformed output, such as extra prose before the JSON, trailing commentary, missing required fields, or minor syntax errors, all of which break naive parsing in production.

How it works

At the loose end, you instruct the model with the exact schema and possibly a few-shot example, and then parse defensively (attempting JSON.parse, retrying on failure, potentially with a repair step). At the strict end, providers offer constrained decoding: given a JSON schema, the API restricts the vocabulary available at each generation step to only tokens that keep the output a valid instance of that schema (this is sometimes implemented as a grammar or finite-state constraint applied directly to the logits before sampling), which makes malformed output structurally impossible rather than just less likely. This constrained approach can occasionally reduce the quality of the content within the structure, since the model's free-text reasoning space is restricted, so some pipelines separate a reasoning step (unconstrained) from a final structured-extraction step (constrained).

When to use it

Use strict schema-constrained JSON mode whenever the provider supports it and you're feeding output directly into code, since it removes an entire class of parsing failures. Use looser prompt-based formatting with defensive parsing when the provider or model doesn't support constrained decoding, or when you need the model to reason freely before producing a final structured summary.

When not to use it

Don't force structured output onto tasks that are fundamentally open-ended or conversational, where the format constraint would hurt the actual content quality with no real downstream parsing need, and be cautious relying purely on 'JSON mode' claims without validating against your exact real-world schema and edge cases, since implementations vary between providers.
keyPoints: Structured output constrains model responses to a defined schema, ranging from loose prompt instructions to strict schema-constrained decoding.
Prompt-only formatting reduces but does not eliminate malformed output; constrained decoding makes invalid output structurally impossible.
Constrained decoding restricts which tokens are allowed at each generation step so the result always matches the schema.
Best fit: use strict JSON mode/schema constraints whenever output feeds directly into code, databases, or function calls.
Avoid forcing structured output onto genuinely open-ended tasks where the constraint would hurt content quality with no parsing benefit.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Your production pipeline parses LLM output as JSON with a simple JSON.parse call, and it fails roughly 3% of the time in production due to extra prose, trailing commas, or truncated output. How would you redesign this to be reliable?
blocks.answer:
I would first check whether the model provider offers a genuine schema-constrained structured output or JSON mode feature, since that class of failure, extra prose around the JSON, malformed syntax, is exactly what constrained decoding is designed to eliminate structurally rather than just reduce in probability.

If that feature is available, I would migrate to it, passing an explicit JSON schema describing the exact fields, types, and required-ness I need, and I would still keep defensive parsing around it, since even structured output features can occasionally hit edge cases like truncation from hitting a max-token limit mid-object.

If constrained decoding isn't available for the model or use case, I would add a layered defense: a strict instruction plus a clear few-shot example showing exactly the desired JSON with no surrounding text, a max-token limit generous enough that legitimate output is never truncated, a JSON-repair step that can fix common issues like trailing commas or an unterminated string before falling back to a full retry, and a retry-with-backoff loop that re-prompts the model (potentially with the parse error included) on failure.

Finally I would add monitoring specifically for the parse failure rate as a first-class metric, since a 3% failure rate silently corrupting downstream data is a production reliability issue, not just a minor prompting quirk, and I'd want alerting if that rate increases after any model or prompt change.
hints: Check for and prefer a genuine schema-constrained output feature over prompt-only formatting.
Add defensive layers: repair step, retry with error feedback, generous token limits.
Treat parse failure rate as a monitored production metric, not a one-off bug.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.explanation: This is the shape of a JSON schema passed to a structured-output API feature: the provider constrains generation so the model can only produce tokens that keep the output a valid instance of exactly this schema, with no extra fields and no missing required ones, instead of relying on the model to correctly follow a prose description.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Relying solely on a prompt instruction like 'respond only in valid JSON' plus a naive JSON.parse call in production, with no schema validation, repair step, or retry logic for the inevitable malformed responses.
blocks.whyItHappens: It works fine in ad-hoc testing with a handful of examples, so the failure rate only becomes visible at production scale and volume, by which point it's already causing silent data corruption or dropped requests.
blocks.correctApproach: Use the strongest structural guarantee available, such as schema-constrained JSON mode, and layer defensive parsing, repair, and retry logic on top regardless, treating the parse failure rate as a monitored metric.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: Prefer strict, provider-level schema constraints over prompt-only formatting wherever available, but always keep a defensive parsing and retry layer, since no single mechanism, prompting or constrained decoding, is a perfect guarantee across every edge case and provider.
keyPoints: Use schema-constrained JSON mode when available instead of relying on prose instructions alone.
Keep a defensive parse-repair-retry layer even when using structured output features.
Monitor parse/schema-validation failure rate in production as a first-class reliability metric.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: Can schema-constrained output guarantee the content is factually correct, not just structurally valid?
blocks.answer: No; constrained decoding only guarantees the output conforms to the schema's shape and types, not that the values are accurate, so factual correctness still needs to be validated separately, through grounding via retrieval, business-logic checks, or human review, independent of the structural guarantee.

title: What Are Embeddings
description: An embedding is a dense numeric vector that represents the meaning of text so that semantically similar inputs end up close together in vector space.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

An embedding is a fixed-length vector of floating-point numbers, typically hundreds to a few thousand dimensions, produced by a trained model such that texts with similar meaning are mapped to vectors that are close together in that high-dimensional space, and texts with different meaning are mapped further apart.

Why this matters

Computers can't directly compare 'meaning'; embeddings turn semantic similarity into a geometric problem, distance or angle between vectors, that's cheap to compute and can be indexed for fast search, which is the foundation for semantic search, recommendation, clustering, deduplication, and retrieval-augmented generation.

How it works

An embedding model, itself usually a transformer encoder, is trained (often via contrastive learning) so that pairs of texts known to be related, such as a question and its correct answer, or two paraphrases, are pulled closer together in vector space during training, while unrelated pairs are pushed apart; the training signal comes from a contrastive loss that rewards small distance for positive pairs and large distance for negative pairs. Once trained, generating an embedding for new text is a single forward pass through the model, pooling the token-level representations (often the final hidden state of a special token, or a mean over all tokens) into one fixed-length vector, with no generation involved at all.

When to use it

Use embeddings whenever you need to compare or search text (or images, audio, etc., with the right model) by semantic similarity rather than exact keyword match, such as building semantic search, recommending similar items, clustering feedback, or retrieving relevant context for RAG.

When not to use it

Don't reach for embeddings when you need exact, deterministic matching, such as looking up a record by an exact ID or SKU, where a plain database index is faster, cheaper, and perfectly precise; embeddings are a fuzzy-matching tool, not a replacement for exact lookups.
keyPoints: An embedding is a fixed-length vector representing text such that similar meanings map to nearby vectors.
Embedding models are typically trained with contrastive learning to pull related pairs together and push unrelated pairs apart in vector space.
Generating an embedding is a single forward pass with no text generation, unlike a normal LLM call.
Best fit: semantic search, recommendation, clustering, deduplication, and RAG retrieval.
Avoid embeddings for exact-match lookups like IDs or SKUs, where a plain database index is more precise and cheaper.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: A teammate suggests using embeddings and cosine similarity to deduplicate a support ticket queue, but is confused about why two tickets with almost no overlapping words end up with a high similarity score, while two tickets sharing several words end up with a lower one. How do you explain this?
blocks.answer:
I would explain that embeddings capture semantic meaning, not surface-level word overlap, because the embedding model was trained to place texts with similar meaning close together in vector space regardless of exact wording, using a contrastive training objective over pairs of related and unrelated texts.

So two tickets like 'my invoice charged me twice this month' and 'I was billed two times for one subscription cycle' can have very high cosine similarity despite almost no shared words, because the model has learned that this combination of concepts, double billing, invoice, subscription, maps to a similar region of the embedding space regardless of the specific vocabulary used.

Conversely, two tickets that share several words, like 'the password reset link expired' and 'the password field on the reset page shows an error,' might land further apart if the model judges the underlying issues, an expired link versus a UI display bug, as meaningfully different problems, even though the word overlap is higher.

This is exactly the intended behavior for deduplication by topic or intent, but I'd flag that if the team specifically also cares about lexical overlap, such as catching duplicate tickets that mention a specific order number or exact error code, pure embedding similarity might miss or under-weight that, so a hybrid approach combining embedding similarity with exact-match or keyword signals for known-important fields would likely give more reliable deduplication than embeddings alone.
hints: Explain that embeddings capture meaning, not lexical overlap.
Give a concrete example where word overlap and semantic similarity diverge in both directions.
Recommend a hybrid approach if exact identifiers or codes matter for the dedup task.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.code:
from openai import OpenAI
import numpy as np

client = OpenAI()

def embed(text):
    response = client.embeddings.create(
        model="text-embedding-3-small",
        input=text
    )
    return np.array(response.data[0].embedding)

v1 = embed("my invoice charged me twice this month")
v2 = embed("I was billed two times for one subscription cycle")

cosine_similarity = np.dot(v1, v2) / (np.linalg.norm(v1) * np.linalg.norm(v2))
print(cosine_similarity)  # expect a high score despite little word overlap
blocks.explanation: Each call to the embeddings endpoint returns a fixed-length vector for the input text with no generation involved; comparing two such vectors with cosine similarity gives a numeric measure of semantic closeness that's usually high for these two sentences despite sharing almost no words.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Describing embeddings as 'a way to turn words into numbers' without explaining that the numbers are trained to encode semantic similarity, or confusing embeddings with simple techniques like one-hot encoding or bag-of-words.
blocks.whyItHappens: Both embeddings and older techniques like one-hot encoding turn text into numeric vectors, so without emphasizing the learned, similarity-preserving structure, the explanation sounds identical to much simpler, purely mechanical text-to-number schemes.
blocks.correctApproach: Emphasize that embeddings are learned representations, trained so that semantic similarity corresponds to vector closeness, unlike one-hot or bag-of-words vectors which carry no notion of meaning or similarity at all.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: Validate an embedding model on your actual domain before committing to it, since general-purpose embedding models can perform noticeably differently on specialized text like legal, medical, or code content, and consider hybrid approaches when exact-match signals matter alongside semantic similarity.
keyPoints: Benchmark embedding model quality on your specific domain and task rather than assuming a general-purpose model transfers perfectly.
Use consistent embedding models across your indexing and querying pipeline; mixing models produces meaningless similarity scores.
Combine embedding similarity with exact-match or keyword signals when precise identifiers matter to the use case.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: Can you compare embeddings generated by two different models directly?
blocks.answer: No, not meaningfully; different embedding models are trained independently with different architectures, dimensions, and training objectives, so their vector spaces aren't aligned, and comparing a vector from one model against a vector from another produces a number with no reliable semantic meaning.

title: Similarity Metrics
description: Cosine similarity, dot product and Euclidean distance each answer how close two vectors are slightly differently, and the embedding model you use usually dictates which one to pick.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors, ignoring their magnitude, and ranges from -1 to 1, with 1 meaning identical direction; dot product measures both the angle and the magnitude of the two vectors combined; Euclidean distance measures the straight-line distance between the two vector endpoints in space, where smaller means more similar.

Why this matters

Picking the wrong metric for a given embedding model can silently degrade retrieval quality, because different embedding models are trained (and their internal loss functions optimized) with a specific metric in mind, and the vector magnitudes they produce aren't necessarily meaningful or comparable across items unless the training objective made them so.

How it works

If an embedding model is trained with normalized vectors (unit length) and a cosine-based or dot-product-based contrastive loss, cosine similarity and dot product actually produce the same ranking of results, since dot product equals cosine similarity times the product of magnitudes, and if all vectors have magnitude 1, that product term is constant. Some models are trained so magnitude itself carries meaningful signal (for example, representing confidence or specificity), in which case dot product (which is sensitive to magnitude) can outperform cosine similarity (which discards it) for that specific model. Euclidean distance is common for embeddings trained with a distance-based loss (like triplet loss with L2 distance) and is mathematically related to cosine similarity for normalized vectors, but is often less used for general-purpose text embeddings than cosine or dot product.

When to use it

Default to the similarity metric explicitly recommended by the embedding model's documentation, since that's what its training objective was actually optimized for; cosine similarity is the safest general default when unsure, particularly for normalized embeddings.

When not to use it

Don't mix and match metrics across models, or switch metrics casually assuming they're interchangeable, since even mathematically related metrics can rank results differently when vector magnitudes vary meaningfully across items, and always re-validate retrieval quality empirically after any metric change.
keyPoints: Cosine similarity measures angle only; dot product measures angle and magnitude; Euclidean distance measures straight-line distance.
For unit-normalized vectors, cosine similarity and dot product produce identical rankings, since magnitude becomes a constant factor.
The correct metric is usually dictated by what the embedding model was actually trained and optimized against.
Best fit: use the metric explicitly recommended by the embedding model's own documentation; cosine is the safest general default.
Avoid mixing metrics across different models or assuming metrics are interchangeable without validating retrieval quality.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Your vector database defaults to Euclidean distance, but the embedding model provider's documentation recommends cosine similarity, and your retrieval quality has been mediocre. How would you investigate and address this?
blocks.answer:
I would first confirm whether this mismatch is actually causing a problem, since for unit-normalized vectors, Euclidean distance and cosine similarity produce mathematically equivalent rankings; if the vectors aren't normalized, though, Euclidean distance will be sensitive to magnitude differences between vectors in a way that may not correspond to the semantic similarity the model was actually trained to represent.

My first concrete step would be to check whether the embedding vectors coming out of the model are unit-normalized; if they're not, I'd either normalize them before insertion into the vector database, or switch the vector database's configured distance metric to cosine similarity (most vector databases support choosing the metric per index) or to dot product on pre-normalized vectors, matching whatever the model's documentation recommends.

After making that change, I would re-run our retrieval evaluation set, a set of queries with known relevant documents, and compare retrieval accuracy (such as recall@k) before and after the metric change, rather than assuming the fix worked just because it matches documentation.

If mediocre retrieval persists even after aligning the metric, I'd widen the investigation to other likely causes: chunking strategy, whether the embedding model is actually a good fit for the domain, and whether a reranking step is needed on top of raw vector similarity.
hints: Check whether vectors are normalized before assuming Euclidean vs cosine matters.
Align the vector database's configured metric with what the embedding model's docs recommend.
Validate the fix with a real retrieval evaluation set, not just assumption.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.explanation: The three metrics are related but not interchangeable in general; the comment captures the key special case, unit-normalized vectors, where cosine similarity and dot product become mathematically identical, which is why checking normalization is the first diagnostic step when a metric mismatch is suspected.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Treating cosine similarity, dot product, and Euclidean distance as interchangeable 'similarity scores' and picking whichever the vector database defaults to, without checking what the embedding model was actually trained and validated against.
blocks.whyItHappens: All three metrics produce a single number that intuitively represents 'closeness,' so without digging into the math, they look like arbitrary implementation choices rather than choices tied to how the specific model was trained.
blocks.correctApproach: Check the embedding model's documentation for its recommended similarity metric, verify whether its output vectors are normalized, and configure the vector database's distance metric to match, validating with a real retrieval evaluation afterward.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: Always match the similarity metric to what the embedding model was trained and documented for, verify vector normalization explicitly, and validate any metric or normalization change against a real retrieval evaluation set rather than trusting intuition.
keyPoints: Use the similarity metric explicitly recommended in the embedding model's own documentation.
Check whether embedding vectors are unit-normalized, since that determines whether cosine and dot product are equivalent.
Validate retrieval quality empirically with recall@k or similar metrics after any metric or normalization change.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: Why do many vector databases default to cosine similarity for text embeddings?
blocks.answer: Because most modern text embedding models are trained with contrastive losses over normalized vectors where direction, not magnitude, is what encodes semantic meaning, so cosine similarity, which ignores magnitude entirely, tends to be the safest general-purpose default across many popular embedding models.

title: Vector Databases
description: A vector database indexes embeddings for fast approximate nearest-neighbor search at scale, trading a little recall for the speed a linear scan cannot provide.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

A vector database stores embedding vectors alongside metadata and builds an index specifically designed to answer 'find the k most similar vectors to this query vector' quickly, using approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) algorithms rather than comparing the query against every stored vector one by one.

Why this matters

A brute-force linear scan, computing similarity against every vector in the collection, is exact but scales linearly with dataset size; at millions of vectors this becomes too slow for interactive applications, so vector databases trade a small amount of recall (the chance of missing the true nearest neighbor) for large gains in query speed, which is the right trade-off for the vast majority of semantic search and RAG use cases.

How it works

Common ANN algorithms include HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs), which builds a multi-layer graph structure where each vector is connected to a handful of nearby vectors, letting a query navigate down through coarser to finer layers to quickly reach a close neighborhood without visiting most of the dataset, and IVF (Inverted File Index), which clusters vectors into buckets ahead of time and only searches the buckets closest to the query vector, rather than every vector in the collection. These indexes are approximate: they can miss the true single best match in exchange for being orders of magnitude faster than an exact scan, and the recall-versus-speed trade-off is usually a tunable parameter (like the number of graph connections in HNSW, or number of buckets searched in IVF). Vector databases also typically support filtering by metadata (like 'only search documents where category = X') combined with the vector search, which naive brute-force implementations often handle less efficiently.

When to use it

Use a dedicated vector database, or a vector index feature within an existing database, once your embedding collection is large enough, or your latency requirements tight enough, that a brute-force scan is measurably too slow, or once you need metadata filtering combined with vector search at scale.

When not to use it

For small collections, tens of thousands of vectors or fewer, a brute-force in-memory scan is often simpler to operate, perfectly fast enough, and exact, so don't add the operational complexity of a dedicated vector database before you've confirmed you actually need the scale it provides.
keyPoints: Vector databases use approximate nearest-neighbor algorithms, like HNSW or IVF, to avoid comparing a query against every stored vector.
ANN search trades a small amount of recall for large gains in query speed at scale, which is the right trade-off for most use cases.
HNSW builds a navigable multi-layer graph; IVF clusters vectors into buckets and searches only the closest ones.
Best fit: large embedding collections or tight latency requirements where brute-force scanning becomes too slow.
Avoid the operational overhead of a dedicated vector database for small collections where a brute-force scan is already fast enough.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Your RAG application's vector search occasionally misses a document that a manual check confirms should have been the top result. A teammate assumes this means the embedding model is broken. What would you check first?
blocks.answer:
I would first separate two very different possible causes: an embedding quality problem, where the model itself doesn't represent that document's meaning well relative to the query, versus an approximate-search recall problem, where the correct document has a good embedding but the ANN index simply didn't surface it among the searched candidates.

My first check would be to run an exact, brute-force similarity search (a linear scan over all vectors) for that specific query, outside the ANN index, and see whether the expected document actually ranks highly under the exact computation. If it does rank highly under exact search but was missed by the ANN index, that points squarely at an approximate-search recall issue, not an embedding model issue.

If that's confirmed, I would look at the ANN index's tunable recall parameters, such as the number of graph connections and search-time exploration factor in HNSW, or the number of buckets searched in IVF, and adjust them to trade some query speed for higher recall, then re-test.

Only if the document genuinely doesn't rank highly even under an exact similarity computation would I escalate to investigating the embedding model itself, or the chunking and text preprocessing that produced that document's embedding in the first place, since that's a different, more fundamental problem than an index tuning issue.
hints: Separate embedding-quality problems from approximate-search recall problems.
Use an exact brute-force search as a diagnostic baseline before blaming the model.
Tune ANN recall parameters rather than assuming the embedding model needs replacing.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

def brute_force_search(query_vec, vectors, k=5):
    # exact, O(n) baseline used to sanity-check ANN index recall
    sims = vectors @ query_vec / (
        np.linalg.norm(vectors, axis=1) * np.linalg.norm(query_vec)
    )
    top_k = np.argsort(-sims)[:k]
    return top_k, sims[top_k]

# Compare this exact result against the vector database's
# approximate result for the same query to isolate whether a
# missing document is an embedding problem or an ANN recall problem.
blocks.explanation: This brute-force scan is intentionally simple and exact; it exists purely as a diagnostic ground truth to compare against a vector database's approximate results, which is the fastest way to isolate whether a retrieval miss comes from the embedding itself or from the ANN index's approximation.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Assuming a vector database always returns the mathematically exact nearest neighbors, and not realizing that most production vector search is approximate by design, which can explain retrieval misses that have nothing to do with the embedding model itself.
blocks.whyItHappens: Vector database documentation often emphasizes accuracy and relevance in marketing terms without foregrounding that the underlying algorithm is an approximate one with a tunable recall trade-off.
blocks.correctApproach: Understand that ANN search trades some recall for speed by design, know how to run an exact baseline for comparison, and know which tunable parameters exist to trade some of that speed back for higher recall when needed.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: Choose and tune a vector database's ANN parameters based on measured recall against an exact baseline for your actual data distribution, and only add a dedicated vector database once collection size or latency requirements genuinely demand it.
keyPoints: Benchmark ANN recall against an exact brute-force baseline on representative queries before trusting default settings.
Tune index parameters (e.g. HNSW connections, IVF bucket count) to trade speed for recall based on actual requirements.
Avoid adopting a dedicated vector database before confirming a brute-force scan is genuinely too slow for your scale.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: Why not always use an exact nearest-neighbor search if it's more accurate?
blocks.answer: Because exact search scales linearly with the number of vectors, so at millions or billions of vectors, query latency becomes far too slow for interactive applications; approximate methods like HNSW achieve sub-linear query time by giving up a small, usually acceptable, amount of recall in exchange for orders of magnitude faster search.

title: Chunking Strategies
description: Chunking splits source documents into retrievable pieces, and the size, overlap and boundary rules you choose directly control retrieval quality.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

Chunking is the process of splitting a source document into smaller pieces before embedding each piece separately, since embedding an entire long document into one vector tends to blur together many different topics or facts into a single, less useful representation, and because retrieval needs to return pieces small enough to be directly useful in a prompt.

Why this matters

Chunk size and boundaries directly determine retrieval quality: chunks that are too large dilute the embedding's specificity (a 2,000-word chunk covering five different subtopics produces a vector that's a blurry average of all of them, making it harder for a query about one specific subtopic to match strongly) and waste context tokens with irrelevant surrounding text, while chunks that are too small lose necessary context (a sentence fragment embedded alone may not carry enough meaning to match the right query, or may match spuriously because it's ambiguous out of context).

How it works

Fixed-size chunking splits text every N tokens or characters, often with some overlap between consecutive chunks (like 10-20%) so information near a chunk boundary isn't completely lost from either side; it's simple to implement but can cut sentences or ideas in half arbitrarily. Structure-aware chunking splits along natural document boundaries instead, such as paragraphs, sections, or markdown headers, which keeps semantically coherent units together, and works especially well when source documents have reliable structure (like documentation with headers, or code split by function). Semantic chunking goes further, using embedding similarity between adjacent sentences to detect topic shifts and splitting right at those boundaries rather than at a fixed size, which produces more topically coherent chunks at the cost of extra preprocessing complexity and compute.

When to use it

Use structure-aware chunking by default whenever your source documents have reliable structure (headers, paragraphs, sections), since it's cheap and usually outperforms naive fixed-size splitting; add overlap between chunks to reduce the chance of losing context right at a boundary; consider semantic chunking for high-value use cases where retrieval accuracy justifies the added preprocessing cost.

When not to use it

Avoid extremely large chunks (whole documents) for retrieval when a query typically needs only one small, specific fact, since it wastes prompt tokens and dilutes the embedding, and avoid extremely small chunks (single sentences with no surrounding context) for content whose meaning depends heavily on nearby sentences, since the fragment alone may not carry enough signal to embed or match well.
keyPoints: Chunking splits documents into smaller retrievable pieces because whole-document embeddings blur multiple topics into one diluted vector.
Chunk size is a direct trade-off: too large dilutes specificity and wastes tokens, too small loses necessary surrounding context.
Structure-aware chunking (paragraphs, headers, sections) generally outperforms naive fixed-size splitting for well-structured documents.
Best fit: structure-aware chunking with modest overlap as the default; semantic chunking for high-value use cases justifying extra cost.
Avoid whole-document chunks for narrow factual queries, and avoid context-free single-sentence chunks for content whose meaning depends on surrounding text.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Your RAG system over technical documentation retrieves chunks that are topically related but frequently cut off mid-explanation, missing the actual answer that appears just after the chunk boundary. How would you diagnose and fix the chunking approach?
blocks.answer:
I would start by inspecting the actual chunking configuration currently in use; if it's fixed-size chunking by token or character count with little or no overlap, that's a strong and very common candidate explanation, since fixed-size boundaries have no awareness of where one idea or explanation ends and another begins, so they routinely cut a relevant explanation exactly at the chunk boundary.

Given that the source is technical documentation, which typically has strong inherent structure like headers, sections, and code blocks, I would switch to structure-aware chunking that splits along those natural boundaries, such as one chunk per subsection or per header-delimited block, so a complete explanation is much more likely to stay within a single chunk rather than being arbitrarily split.

I would also add a reasonable overlap between adjacent chunks, even with structure-aware splitting, so that content immediately before or after a section boundary is available in the neighboring chunk as well, catching cases where an explanation genuinely spans a structural boundary.

To validate the fix, I'd build a small evaluation set of real questions and the specific chunk (or chunks) that should be retrieved to answer each fully, and I would explicitly test whether the retrieved chunk contains the complete relevant explanation, not just whether it's topically related, before and after the chunking change, since 'topically related but incomplete' is exactly the failure mode described and needs to be measured directly, not just inferred from vibes.
hints: Diagnose whether current chunking is naive fixed-size with no structural awareness.
Recommend structure-aware chunking aligned to the document's natural sections/headers.
Build an eval set testing chunk completeness, not just topical relevance.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.explanation: The first function respects the document's own structure instead of an arbitrary character count, keeping each header together with its content; the second adds light overlap so context immediately preceding a section boundary is still available in the next chunk, reducing the chance a relevant explanation gets split awkwardly.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Picking a single fixed chunk size (like 500 tokens) as a blanket default for every document type and never revisiting it, without considering the source document's structure or testing retrieval completeness.
blocks.whyItHappens: Fixed-size chunking is the simplest to implement and is what most introductory RAG tutorials demonstrate first, so it's easy to treat as a permanent default rather than a starting point to improve on.
blocks.correctApproach: Match the chunking strategy to the document's actual structure, add overlap to reduce boundary loss, and validate retrieval completeness, not just topical relevance, against a real evaluation set.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: Treat chunking strategy as a tunable, testable part of the RAG pipeline rather than a one-time preprocessing detail, and measure retrieval completeness directly against real questions rather than assuming any single chunk size or splitting rule generalizes across document types.
keyPoints: Prefer structure-aware chunking over naive fixed-size splitting whenever source documents have reliable structure.
Add modest overlap between chunks to reduce information loss right at chunk boundaries.
Evaluate chunking changes against real questions checking for complete, not just topically relevant, retrieved content.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up

blocks.answer: No; the right chunk size depends on the nature of the source content, the typical granularity of user queries, and the embedding model's own behavior, so it should be tuned and validated per use case with a real retrieval evaluation set rather than copied from a generic recommendation.

title: Hybrid Search
description: Hybrid search combines keyword (lexical) search with vector (semantic) search so exact terms like IDs and acronyms are not lost to purely semantic matching.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

Hybrid search runs both a lexical (keyword) search, typically using an algorithm like BM25 that scores documents by exact and near-exact term overlap with the query, and a semantic (vector/embedding) search over the same documents, then combines the two ranked result sets, usually with a weighted score fusion or a rank-fusion algorithm like Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), into one final ranking.

Why this matters

Pure semantic search is excellent at matching meaning even with completely different wording, but it can genuinely underperform on queries containing exact identifiers, product codes, acronyms, rare technical terms, or proper nouns, because an embedding model trained primarily on natural-language semantics may not encode small distinguishing details, like a specific error code or SKU, precisely enough for those tokens to dominate the similarity score; two documents differing only in an exact code might embed almost identically. Keyword search, by contrast, matches exact tokens precisely but completely misses paraphrases and synonyms, which is the opposite failure mode. Combining both covers each other's blind spots.

How it works

BM25, the standard lexical scoring algorithm, ranks documents based on term frequency (how often a query term appears in a document) and inverse document frequency (how rare that term is across the whole collection), with normalization for document length, so a document containing a rare, exact query term ranks highly regardless of surrounding semantic context. The vector search independently returns its own ranked list based on embedding similarity. Reciprocal Rank Fusion combines two or more ranked lists by giving each document a score based on 1/(rank + k) in each list and summing across lists, so a document that ranks well in either list (not necessarily both) still surfaces near the top of the combined ranking, without needing the two very differently-scaled scores (BM25 scores and cosine similarities) to be directly comparable.

When to use it

Use hybrid search whenever your query distribution includes a meaningful share of exact-match-sensitive queries, such as product codes, error messages, names, acronyms, or technical jargon, alongside more natural-language queries, which describes the majority of real-world enterprise search and RAG applications.

When not to use it

For a narrow use case where queries are reliably natural-language paraphrases with no meaningful exact-term matching need (like open-ended conversational recall), pure semantic search alone may be simpler to operate and sufficient, so validate with real query logs before adding the operational complexity of maintaining both a lexical and vector index plus a fusion step.
keyPoints: Hybrid search combines lexical (BM25-style keyword) search and semantic (embedding) search into one ranking.
Semantic search alone can underperform on exact identifiers, codes, and rare technical terms that pure embedding similarity doesn't distinguish well.
Reciprocal Rank Fusion combines differently-scaled ranked lists by summing 1/(rank+k) scores, avoiding the need to directly compare BM25 and cosine scores.
Best fit: query distributions mixing exact-match-sensitive terms (codes, names, jargon) with natural-language paraphrases.
Avoid the added operational complexity of hybrid search if real query logs show no meaningful exact-match need.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Users report that searching your internal documentation for a specific error code like 'ERR-4471' returns semantically related but unhelpful articles, never the exact one describing that code. How would you diagnose and fix this?
blocks.answer:
I would first confirm the hypothesis directly: the current system is presumably pure vector search, and an embedding model, trained primarily to capture general semantic meaning, may not reliably encode a specific alphanumeric code as a strongly distinguishing feature, so two articles about similar categories of errors, one of which happens to mention ERR-4471 and one which doesn't, can end up with very similar embeddings and therefore similar ranking, causing the exact match to get buried among semantically-similar-but-wrong results.

The fix I'd recommend is adding a lexical search index, such as BM25 over the same document set, alongside the existing vector search. BM25 would score the document containing the literal string 'ERR-4471' far higher than documents that don't contain it at all, specifically because BM25 rewards exact term matches, especially for rare terms with high inverse document frequency, which an error code like this would have.

I would combine the two ranked lists using a rank-fusion approach like Reciprocal Rank Fusion rather than trying to merge raw BM25 and cosine similarity scores directly, since those scores live on completely different scales and aren't directly comparable; RRF lets a document that ranks first in the lexical list surface near the top of the combined result even if its semantic rank is mediocre.

To validate, I would build a small test set of exact-code queries with known correct documents, plus a set of natural-language paraphrase queries, and confirm the hybrid approach improves accuracy on the code-lookup queries without regressing accuracy on the paraphrase queries, since the goal is to cover both failure modes, not trade one for the other.
hints: Diagnose why pure vector search underperforms on exact codes specifically.
Recommend adding BM25-style lexical search rather than tweaking the embedding model.
Use rank fusion (like RRF) instead of merging incompatible raw scores, and validate on both query types.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.explanation: Reciprocal Rank Fusion sidesteps the problem of BM25 and cosine similarity scores being on incompatible scales by only using each list's rank positions; a document that ranks highly in even one of the lists gets a meaningful boost in the combined score.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Trying to fix poor exact-match retrieval by only tuning the embedding model or the chunking strategy, instead of recognizing that pure semantic search has a structural blind spot for exact identifiers that a lexical search component is specifically designed to cover.
blocks.whyItHappens: Once a RAG pipeline is built around vector search, it's natural to look for fixes within that same system (better embeddings, better chunks) rather than considering that a fundamentally different retrieval mechanism might be missing entirely.
blocks.correctApproach: Recognize exact-match-sensitive query failures as a signal to add a lexical search component and fuse it with vector search, rather than trying to force semantic search alone to solve a problem it's structurally weaker at.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: Add hybrid search when real query logs show a meaningful share of exact-match-sensitive queries, use rank fusion rather than merging incompatible raw scores, and validate improvements separately against both exact-match and paraphrase query sets to confirm neither regresses.
keyPoints: Analyze real query logs to confirm exact-match-sensitive queries are common enough to justify hybrid search's added complexity.
Use rank-fusion methods like RRF rather than naively combining BM25 and cosine similarity scores.
Test both exact-match and natural-language paraphrase query sets to confirm hybrid search improves one without regressing the other.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: Why not just directly combine BM25 scores and cosine similarity scores with a weighted average instead of using rank fusion?
blocks.answer: Because BM25 scores and cosine similarities live on entirely different, non-comparable scales that can also shift depending on the query and collection, so a fixed weighted average is fragile and hard to tune reliably; rank-based fusion methods like RRF avoid this by only relying on each list's relative ordering, which is far more stable across different queries and collections.
