title: What Is RAG and Why It Matters
description: RAG grounds a model's answer in retrieved documents at request time, which reduces hallucination and lets an application answer from private or fast-changing data without retraining.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is an architecture where, before generating a response, the system retrieves relevant documents or passages from an external knowledge source, usually via embedding similarity search, and inserts them into the model's prompt as grounding context, so the model answers based on that retrieved evidence rather than relying solely on facts encoded in its trained weights.

Why this matters

A model's weights encode a frozen snapshot of whatever it saw during training, so it has no way to know about private company data it never saw, or about anything that changed after its training cutoff, and left to answer from memory alone, it will often generate a plausible-sounding but wrong or outdated answer rather than admitting uncertainty. RAG sidesteps this by handing the model the actual current, relevant source text as part of the prompt, on every single request, which grounds the answer in retrievable, verifiable, and easily updatable evidence instead of the model's static internal knowledge, and it does this without the cost or latency of retraining or fine-tuning every time the underlying data changes.

How it works

At indexing time, source documents are chunked, embedded, and stored in a vector store (often alongside a lexical index for hybrid search). At query time, the user's question is embedded with the same model, the vector store returns the most similar chunks, those chunks are inserted into the prompt (often after a reranking step), and the LLM generates its answer conditioned on both the question and that retrieved context, ideally with instructions to answer only from the provided context and to say so explicitly when the answer isn't present.

When to use it

Use RAG whenever an application needs to answer questions grounded in a specific, private, or frequently changing body of knowledge, such as internal documentation, customer data, product catalogs, or news, where fine-tuning would be too slow, too expensive, or simply the wrong tool for injecting per-request factual grounding.

When not to use it

Don't reach for RAG when the task doesn't actually depend on external factual grounding, such as purely creative writing, or general reasoning tasks the model already handles well from its trained knowledge, since adding retrieval there only adds latency, cost, and irrelevant context with no accuracy benefit.
keyPoints: RAG retrieves relevant documents at request time and inserts them into the prompt so generation is grounded in retrieved evidence.
It solves the fundamental limitation that a model's weights are a frozen, static snapshot with no built-in access to private or newly-changed data.
The pipeline is: chunk and embed documents ahead of time, embed the query, retrieve similar chunks, then generate conditioned on question plus retrieved context.
Best fit: applications needing grounded answers over private, specific, or frequently changing knowledge.
Avoid RAG for tasks with no real dependency on external factual grounding, where it adds cost and latency with no benefit.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: A stakeholder asks why you can't just fine-tune the model on the company's internal wiki instead of building a RAG pipeline, since 'the model would just know the answers directly.' How do you respond?
blocks.answer:
I would explain that fine-tuning bakes knowledge into the model's weights at a specific point in time, which creates two real problems for a use case like an internal wiki: the wiki changes constantly, so the fine-tuned model would go stale the moment any page is updated, and re-fine-tuning on every change is far slower and more expensive than updating a document in a database, which is instant.

There's also a subtler issue: fine-tuning on factual documents doesn't reliably teach a model to recall those facts precisely on demand the way people often assume; the model may still blend, paraphrase, or hallucinate details rather than reproducing the source faithfully, whereas RAG hands the model the actual current source text directly in the prompt, so it can quote or closely follow it, and we can literally show users which source document backed a given answer, which fine-tuning can't provide at all.

Cost is another factor: RAG only requires embedding the wiki content once (and re-embedding changed pages incrementally), which is cheap, versus a genuine fine-tuning run, which requires meaningfully more compute, MLOps investment, and time to iterate.

I would frame the actual choice as: use RAG for grounding the model in specific, current, verifiable content like the wiki, and reserve fine-tuning, if we ever need it, for changing the model's overall behavior, tone, or task-specific skills, which is a different problem than keeping it up to date on facts.
hints: Contrast staleness and update cost between fine-tuning and RAG.
Note that fine-tuning doesn't reliably guarantee faithful factual recall the way direct retrieval does.
Reframe fine-tuning's actual strength (behavior/style) versus RAG's strength (current, verifiable grounding).

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.explanation: This is the minimal RAG loop: embed the question, retrieve the most similar chunks from the vector store, and hand them to the model with an explicit instruction to answer only from that context, which is what grounds the response in retrievable, current source material instead of the model's static trained knowledge.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Describing RAG as simply 'giving the model more data' or 'making the model smarter,' without explaining that it specifically addresses staleness and lack of access to private data by injecting retrieved evidence into the prompt at request time.
blocks.whyItHappens: RAG's end effect, better and more current answers, sounds similar to generic descriptions of improving a model, which obscures the specific mechanism (retrieval plus prompt injection at request time) that actually produces the improvement.
blocks.correctApproach: Explain the concrete mechanism: documents are chunked, embedded, and indexed ahead of time; at request time the query is embedded, similar chunks are retrieved, and those chunks are inserted directly into the prompt so the model generates its answer conditioned on that specific, current evidence.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: Reserve RAG for genuine factual-grounding needs over specific, private, or changing data, instruct the model explicitly to answer only from retrieved context and to admit when it can't, and validate that answers are actually traceable back to the retrieved sources rather than assuming grounding alone eliminates hallucination.
keyPoints: Instruct the model explicitly to answer only from provided context and to say when the context doesn't contain the answer.
Keep the underlying index up to date incrementally rather than treating RAG as a one-time setup.
Validate that generated answers are actually traceable to the retrieved sources, since RAG reduces but does not eliminate hallucination risk.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: Does RAG completely eliminate hallucination?
blocks.answer: No; RAG significantly reduces hallucination by grounding answers in retrieved evidence, but a model can still misread, misquote, or over-generalize from the retrieved context, or blend it with unrelated trained knowledge, so hallucination risk is reduced, not eliminated, and should still be monitored and evaluated.

title: The Naive RAG Pipeline
description: A naive RAG pipeline chunks and embeds documents ahead of time, then at query time retrieves the top matches and stuffs them into the prompt before generation.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

The naive (or 'vanilla') RAG pipeline is the simplest end-to-end version of retrieval-augmented generation: split documents into chunks, embed each chunk once and store it in a vector index, and at query time embed the incoming question, retrieve the top-k most similar chunks by vector similarity alone, concatenate them directly into the prompt, and generate an answer, with no reranking, no query rewriting, and no iterative retrieval.

Why this matters

Naive RAG is the right starting point for almost every RAG project because it's fast to build and gives a real baseline to measure against, but it has well-known, predictable failure modes: pure top-k vector similarity retrieval can surface topically related but unhelpful chunks, miss exact-term queries that need lexical matching, retrieve redundant near-duplicate chunks that all say the same thing, or fail on questions requiring information synthesized across multiple, non-adjacent chunks that individually don't look highly similar to the query. Understanding these specific failure modes is what motivates every 'advanced RAG' technique, reranking, hybrid search, query rewriting, as a targeted fix rather than a generic improvement.

How it works

Offline: documents are split into chunks (with a chosen chunking strategy), each chunk is passed through an embedding model, and the resulting vectors plus original chunk text and metadata are stored in a vector index. Online, per request: the user's question is embedded with the same model, the vector index returns the k nearest chunks by similarity, those chunk texts are concatenated (often with instructions and the question) into a single prompt, and that prompt is sent to the LLM to generate the final answer, which is returned to the user, often alongside citations pointing back to the source chunks.

When to use it

Start with naive RAG for any new retrieval-augmented application, since it establishes a working baseline quickly and cheaply, and use its measured failure modes on your actual data and queries to decide which specific advanced technique, if any, is worth the added complexity.

When not to use it

Don't ship naive RAG as the final production system for a use case where evaluation reveals systematic failures, such as consistently missing exact-term queries or being overwhelmed by near-duplicate chunks, without adding the specific targeted fix, hybrid search, reranking, deduplication, that addresses the failure mode you actually observed.
keyPoints: Naive RAG chunks and embeds documents offline, then retrieves top-k similar chunks by vector similarity alone at query time with no reranking or rewriting.
It's the right starting baseline for nearly every RAG project because it's fast and cheap to build and evaluate against.
Known failure modes include missing exact-term matches, redundant near-duplicate retrieval, and failing multi-chunk synthesis questions.
Best fit: as the initial baseline for any new RAG application, to be improved based on observed, measured failures.
Avoid shipping naive RAG unchanged to production once evaluation reveals a systematic, addressable failure mode.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: You built a naive RAG pipeline as a proof of concept and it looked great in a demo, but a broader evaluation on real user questions shows accuracy is inconsistent. How would you approach diagnosing what to fix first?
blocks.answer:
I would resist the urge to add every advanced RAG technique at once, and instead build a proper evaluation set first: a representative sample of real user questions with known correct answers and, ideally, the specific source chunk that should have been retrieved to answer each one correctly.

Running the current naive pipeline against that set, I would separately measure retrieval accuracy, did the correct chunk actually get retrieved in the top-k, and generation accuracy given correct retrieval, did the model answer correctly when the right chunk was present, because these are different failure modes needing different fixes, and conflating them leads to fixing the wrong stage.

If retrieval is the main bottleneck, I would look at the specific pattern of misses: if failures cluster around exact terms, codes, or names, that points to adding hybrid (lexical plus vector) search; if failures cluster around the right topic being retrieved but ranked too low, that points to adding a reranking step; if failures involve needing to synthesize across multiple non-adjacent chunks, that points to chunking or multi-hop retrieval issues rather than a ranking problem.

Only after identifying the dominant, measured failure pattern would I add the corresponding advanced technique, then re-run the same evaluation set to confirm the specific fix actually improved the specific metric it targeted, rather than assuming a general 'better RAG' change helped without re-measuring.
hints: Insist on a real evaluation set separating retrieval accuracy from generation accuracy.
Match the diagnosed failure pattern to a specific advanced technique rather than adding everything at once.
Re-measure after each targeted fix rather than assuming general improvement.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Treating naive RAG as production-ready simply because a demo looked convincing, without building a real evaluation set that separately measures retrieval accuracy and generation accuracy against representative user questions.
blocks.whyItHappens: A handful of manually chosen demo queries tend to be exactly the kind of clean, well-phrased questions naive RAG handles well, which masks failure modes that only appear across the diversity of real user queries at scale.
blocks.correctApproach: Build a representative evaluation set with known correct answers and source chunks, measure retrieval and generation accuracy separately, and only add specific advanced techniques in response to a measured, specific failure pattern.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: Treat naive RAG as an intentional, cheap baseline to measure against, not a placeholder to feel embarrassed about; add complexity, hybrid search, reranking, query rewriting, only in direct response to a specific, measured failure mode observed on real queries.
keyPoints: Build and maintain an evaluation set with known correct answers and source chunks before judging RAG quality.
Measure retrieval accuracy and generation accuracy as separate metrics to isolate which stage needs improvement.
Add advanced RAG techniques incrementally, each targeting a specific, observed failure mode, and re-measure after each change.

blocks.answer: Retrieving chunks that are topically related to the query but don't actually contain the specific fact needed to answer it, often because pure top-k vector similarity favors general topical closeness over the precise, narrow relevance a reranking step is specifically designed to surface.

title: Reranking and Retrieval Quality
description: A reranker re-scores the initial retrieved candidates with a more accurate but slower model, fixing the common case where the right chunk is retrieved but ranked too low to matter.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

Reranking is a second retrieval stage: after an initial, cheap retrieval step (usually vector similarity, sometimes combined with lexical search) returns a wider candidate set, say the top 40 or 100 chunks, a separate, more computationally expensive but more accurate model rescoring only that candidate set, re-ranks them, and only the top few after reranking (say 5-8) are actually passed into the LLM's prompt.

Why this matters

Embedding-based retrieval computes similarity from independently-generated query and document vectors (a 'two-tower' or 'dual-encoder' setup), which is fast because document embeddings can be precomputed and indexed, but it's a comparatively coarse similarity signal since it never lets the query and document interact directly; the right document is often retrieved into the initial candidate set but doesn't necessarily rank in the top few by that coarse similarity alone. A cross-encoder reranker, by contrast, processes the query and each candidate document together, in the same forward pass, letting them directly interact token-by-token, which produces a much more accurate relevance judgment, at the cost of being far too slow to run over an entire large collection, which is exactly why it's only applied to the smaller candidate set the first stage already narrowed down.

How it works

A cross-encoder reranker takes (query, candidate_chunk) pairs as joint input, one pair at a time (or in a batch), runs them through a transformer that attends across both the query and the chunk simultaneously, and outputs a single relevance score per pair; unlike the dual-encoder embedding approach, this joint attention lets the model directly assess fine-grained relevance, like whether the chunk actually answers the specific question, not just whether it's topically similar. Because this is computationally expensive per pair, it's only feasible to run it over the initial stage's narrowed candidate set (tens of documents), not the entire collection (potentially millions).

When to use it

Add a reranking stage whenever evaluation shows that the correct chunk is present somewhere in the initial retrieval candidates but not reliably in the final top-k sent to the LLM, which is one of the most common and highest-leverage RAG quality fixes available.

When not to use it

Skip reranking for latency-critical paths where the added round-trip and compute cost isn't justified, or when evaluation shows the initial retrieval stage is already reliably surfacing the right chunk near the top without it; always validate the decision with a measured recall@k comparison rather than adding reranking reflexively.
keyPoints: Reranking re-scores an initial retrieval candidate set with a more accurate, more expensive cross-encoder model before final selection.
Embedding (dual-encoder) retrieval is fast but coarse because query and document vectors are computed independently, with no direct interaction.
A cross-encoder reranker processes query and candidate jointly, letting them attend to each other for a much more precise relevance judgment.
Best fit: when evaluation shows the correct chunk is retrieved but not reliably ranked near the top by initial vector similarity alone.
Avoid reranking on latency-critical paths, or when measured evaluation shows initial retrieval is already reliable without it.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Your evaluation shows the correct document chunk appears in the top 30 vector search results for 92% of test questions, but only in the top 5 for 61% of them, and your prompt only includes the top 5 chunks. What would you do, and why is this exactly the problem reranking solves?
blocks.answer:
I would recognize this as a textbook case for adding a reranking stage rather than trying to fix it purely by tuning the embedding model or the vector index, because the data itself tells a clear story: the initial retrieval stage is doing its job, the right chunk is present in the candidate pool 92% of the time, but the ranking within that pool isn't precise enough, since it only lands in the final top 5 sent to the LLM 61% of the time.

This gap between 'present in a wide candidate set' and 'ranked in the narrow final set' is exactly what reranking is designed to close: I'd widen the initial retrieval to return a larger candidate set, say the top 30 or 50 by vector similarity, since we already know that's enough to have 92% recall, then run a cross-encoder reranker over just that candidate set to get a much more precise relevance ranking, and finally take only the reranker's top 5 to build the final prompt.

Because a cross-encoder lets the query and each candidate chunk directly attend to each other, rather than comparing independently-computed embeddings, it can much more reliably distinguish 'this chunk is topically similar' from 'this chunk actually answers the specific question,' which is precisely the distinction that's failing when a relevant chunk is present but ranked outside the top 5.

After implementing this, I would re-run the same evaluation and specifically check that the top-5-after-reranking recall rises much closer to that 92% ceiling, confirming the fix addressed the actual measured gap rather than assuming it worked.
hints: Recognize the gap between candidate-set recall and top-k recall as the specific signal for reranking.
Explain why cross-encoders resolve fine-grained relevance better than dual-encoder similarity alone.
Re-measure top-k recall after reranking against the wide-candidate-set ceiling to confirm the fix worked.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.code:
def rag_with_reranking(question, embed_fn, vector_store, reranker, llm,
                        initial_k=30, final_k=5):
    query_vector = embed_fn(question)
    candidates = vector_store.search(query_vector, k=initial_k)  # wide, cheap pass

    scored = [
        (chunk, reranker.score(question, chunk.text))  # slow, precise pass
        for chunk in candidates
    ]
    top_chunks = [c for c, _ in sorted(scored, key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)[:final_k]]

    context = "\n\n".join(c.text for c in top_chunks)
    prompt = f"Context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}"
    return llm.generate(prompt)
blocks.explanation: The candidate set is intentionally wider than what's actually sent to the LLM, giving the reranker room to correct the initial ranking; only after the more expensive, more accurate cross-encoder scoring pass does the final top-5 selection happen, which is the core two-stage retrieve-then-rerank pattern.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Trying to fix a low top-k retrieval recall problem by only tuning the embedding model, chunking, or the number of chunks retrieved, without recognizing it as a ranking-precision problem that a reranking stage is specifically designed to solve.
blocks.whyItHappens: The visible symptom, wrong or missing chunks in the final prompt, looks like it could be caused by many parts of the pipeline, and reranking as a distinct, separate stage isn't always the first thing considered without prior exposure to the pattern.
blocks.correctApproach: Diagnose by measuring recall at a wide candidate-set size versus recall at the actual final top-k used in the prompt; a large gap between the two is the specific signal that a reranking stage, not embedding or chunking changes, is the targeted fix.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: Add reranking as a targeted fix once evaluation shows a gap between wide-candidate-set recall and final top-k recall, and always weigh the added latency of the cross-encoder pass against the recall improvement it delivers for your specific latency budget.
keyPoints: Measure recall at a wide candidate-set size versus the actual final top-k to detect the specific gap reranking addresses.
Use a cross-encoder reranker only over the narrowed candidate set, never over the full collection, due to its per-pair compute cost.
Weigh reranking's added latency against its measured recall improvement for your specific application's latency budget.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: Why can't you just use a cross-encoder for the entire retrieval step instead of a two-stage retrieve-then-rerank approach?
blocks.answer: Because a cross-encoder has to process the query jointly with every candidate document in a full forward pass, so its cost scales with the size of the full collection, which is far too slow for real-time search over large document sets; the two-stage approach uses cheap, precomputed embedding similarity to narrow a huge collection down to a small candidate set first, then applies the expensive cross-encoder only to that small set.

title: Agentic RAG and Graph RAG
description: Agentic RAG lets the model decide when and what to retrieve across multiple steps, while graph RAG retrieves through explicit entity relationships instead of flat chunk similarity.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

Agentic RAG replaces the single fixed retrieve-then-generate step with a model-driven loop: the model itself decides whether it needs to retrieve, generates a query (possibly rewriting or decomposing the original question), evaluates whether the retrieved results are sufficient, and can issue additional retrieval calls, potentially against different sources or tools, before producing a final answer. Graph RAG instead builds or leverages a knowledge graph, entities as nodes and their relationships as edges, and retrieves by traversing explicit relationships between entities rather than relying purely on flat chunk-level embedding similarity.

Why this matters

Naive single-shot RAG assumes one retrieval pass with the original (or lightly rewritten) query is enough, but many real questions need multi-hop reasoning ('what did the person who succeeded the CEO mentioned in this report previously work on?') where no single chunk contains the full answer, and flat vector similarity has no notion of the explicit relationship path connecting the needed facts. Agentic RAG addresses this by giving the model the ability to decompose a complex question into sub-queries and retrieve iteratively, while graph RAG addresses a related but distinct problem: representing structured relationships (org charts, product hierarchies, dependency graphs) explicitly, so retrieval can follow 'who reports to whom' or 'which component depends on which' relationships that flat text similarity captures poorly or not at all.

How it works

Agentic RAG is typically implemented with an LLM that has retrieval exposed as a callable tool; the model's own reasoning loop decides to call it, inspects the returned chunks, and either answers or issues another, refined retrieval call, sometimes explicitly planning a sequence of sub-questions first. Graph RAG requires an extra offline step beyond simple chunking: extracting entities and relationships from source documents (often using an LLM itself) to build a graph structure, then at query time, retrieval can combine vector similarity (to find a relevant starting entity or passage) with graph traversal (to pull in directly connected, relevant entities and facts) rather than relying purely on flat text similarity.

When to use it

Use agentic RAG when questions in your domain frequently require multi-step reasoning or synthesizing information that no single retrieval pass reliably surfaces together. Use graph RAG when your domain has genuinely structured, relationship-heavy data, organizational hierarchies, product dependency graphs, citation networks, where explicit relationships materially improve retrieval over flat similarity.

When not to use it

Avoid agentic RAG's added latency and complexity, since it requires multiple model calls per query, when most questions in your domain are answerable from a single well-retrieved chunk; avoid graph RAG's significant added indexing complexity and cost, extracting entities and relationships is itself an error-prone LLM task, when your data doesn't have meaningfully exploitable relational structure beyond plain text similarity.
keyPoints: Agentic RAG lets the model iteratively decide when and what to retrieve, decomposing complex questions into multiple retrieval steps.
Graph RAG retrieves through explicit entity relationships in a knowledge graph, rather than relying purely on flat chunk-level similarity.
Both address multi-hop questions that single-shot flat vector retrieval cannot answer well, via different mechanisms.
Best fit for agentic RAG: domains with frequent multi-step reasoning questions; best fit for graph RAG: domains with genuine structured relational data.
Avoid both when most questions are answerable from a single well-retrieved chunk, given their added latency, cost, and implementation complexity.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Your naive RAG system fails on questions like 'which vendors used by Team A are also flagged as high-risk in the compliance database,' where the answer requires combining facts from two different, unrelated-looking source documents. How would you approach fixing this, and would you reach for agentic RAG, graph RAG, or something else?
blocks.answer:
I would first recognize that this is a multi-hop question: it requires retrieving one fact (which vendors Team A uses) and then using that result to retrieve a second, dependent fact (which of those specific vendors are flagged high-risk), and no single chunk in either source document contains the combined answer, so no amount of tuning a single flat retrieval pass will reliably solve it.

Given that the relationship here, vendors used by a team, and vendors flagged in a separate compliance system, is genuinely structured and relational rather than just topically related text, I would lean toward a graph RAG approach if this kind of cross-referencing question is common in the domain: representing teams, vendors, and risk flags as entities and relationships would let retrieval directly traverse from Team A to its vendors to their risk status, which is a much more reliable mechanism than hoping vector similarity happens to surface the right combination of chunks.

If building and maintaining a knowledge graph is too large an investment for how often this specific pattern occurs, I would consider agentic RAG as a lighter-weight alternative: the model could first retrieve Team A's vendor list, then issue a second retrieval call specifically querying the compliance database for those vendor names, effectively performing the multi-hop reasoning through iterative tool calls rather than a pre-built graph structure.

I would validate whichever approach I choose against a set of real multi-hop questions from this domain, since both graph RAG and agentic RAG add real implementation and latency cost, and I want to confirm the chosen approach actually resolves this specific failure pattern before committing to it as a permanent architecture change.
hints: Diagnose this specifically as a multi-hop, cross-document reasoning failure, not a chunking or embedding problem.
Weigh graph RAG (explicit relationships) against agentic RAG (iterative tool-based retrieval) based on how structured and recurring the pattern is.
Validate the chosen approach against real multi-hop questions before committing to the added complexity.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.explanation: Unlike naive RAG's single fixed retrieve-then-generate call, this loop lets the model itself decide, at each step, whether it has enough context to answer or needs to issue another, model-generated retrieval query, which is what enables multi-hop questions to be answered through iterative retrieval rather than one static pass.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Reaching for agentic RAG or graph RAG as a default 'more advanced equals better' upgrade without first confirming the observed failures are actually multi-hop or relationship-structure problems that a single-shot flat retrieval genuinely cannot solve.
blocks.whyItHappens: Both techniques are prominently discussed as state-of-the-art improvements to RAG, which can make them feel like a general upgrade path rather than targeted fixes for specific, diagnosable failure patterns.
blocks.correctApproach: Diagnose the specific failure pattern first, single-chunk retrieval misses versus genuinely multi-hop or relationship-dependent questions, and only add agentic or graph RAG's substantial extra complexity and cost when the evaluation clearly shows that specific need.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: Confirm multi-hop or relationship-dependent failures with real evaluation examples before adopting agentic or graph RAG, since both add meaningful latency, cost, and implementation complexity that isn't justified for domains where single-shot flat retrieval already performs well.
keyPoints: Verify failures are genuinely multi-hop or relationship-dependent, not fixable by simpler reranking or chunking improvements, before adopting either technique.
Budget for the added latency of multiple model/retrieval calls in agentic RAG and the added indexing complexity of entity/relationship extraction in graph RAG.
Validate the chosen approach against a dedicated set of multi-hop evaluation questions, not just general accuracy metrics.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: Can agentic RAG and graph RAG be combined?
blocks.answer: Yes; an agentic loop can use graph traversal as one of its available retrieval tools alongside flat vector search, letting the model decide when a question calls for following explicit entity relationships versus when a plain similarity search is sufficient, combining the iterative reasoning of agentic RAG with the structured retrieval precision of graph RAG.

title: Evaluating RAG Quality
description: RAG evaluation has to separately measure retrieval quality and generation quality, because good retrieval with a bad answer looks identical to bad retrieval from the outside.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

A RAG system has (at least) two independent stages that can each fail, retrieval (did the system find the right source content) and generation (did the model produce a correct, faithful answer given that content), and a wrong final answer alone doesn't tell you which stage failed, so RAG evaluation needs metrics that isolate each stage separately, not just an end-to-end 'was the final answer right' check.

Why this matters

If you only measure whether the final answer matches an expected answer, you can't tell whether to fix retrieval (better chunking, hybrid search, reranking) or generation (better prompting, a different model, stricter grounding instructions), and teams that skip this separation often spend significant effort improving the wrong stage of the pipeline based on a misdiagnosis.

How it works

Retrieval quality is typically measured with information-retrieval metrics like recall@k (did the correct source chunk appear anywhere in the top k retrieved results) and precision@k or mean reciprocal rank (how highly was it ranked), computed against a labeled evaluation set of questions paired with their known correct source chunks. Generation quality, given retrieval already succeeded, is measured with metrics like faithfulness or groundedness (does the generated answer actually follow from the provided context, checked either by a human rubric or an LLM-as-judge comparing the answer against the retrieved context) and answer relevance or correctness (does the answer actually address the question, checked against a reference answer or rubric). Frameworks like RAGAS formalize several of these into standard, automatable metrics (context precision, context recall, faithfulness, answer relevance) that can be computed at scale using an LLM judge rather than requiring full manual review for every evaluation run.

When to use it

Build a labeled evaluation set (questions, expected correct source chunks, and reference answers) and run separate retrieval and generation metrics before and after any pipeline change, chunking, embedding model, reranker, prompt, so you can attribute quality changes to the specific component you modified.

When not to use it

Don't rely purely on spot-checking a handful of example queries by eye as your only evaluation method once the system is past the earliest prototyping stage, and don't trust an LLM-as-judge metric blindly without periodically validating its judgments against real human review, since judge models have their own biases and blind spots.
keyPoints: RAG evaluation must separate retrieval quality (recall@k, precision@k, MRR) from generation quality (faithfulness, answer relevance).
A wrong final answer alone doesn't reveal which stage, retrieval or generation, actually failed.
Faithfulness/groundedness checks whether the answer actually follows from the retrieved context, distinct from whether it addresses the question at all.
Best fit: maintain a labeled eval set (questions, correct source chunks, reference answers) and measure both stages before/after any pipeline change.
Avoid relying solely on ad hoc spot-checking or blindly trusting an LLM judge without periodic human validation.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: After swapping in a new embedding model, your team sees the end-to-end 'answer correctness' metric drop, and someone concludes the new embedding model is worse. How would you determine whether that conclusion is actually justified?
blocks.answer:
I would push back on drawing that conclusion from the end-to-end metric alone, since a drop in overall answer correctness could come from a retrieval regression, the new embedding model surfacing worse source chunks, or a generation-stage issue that has nothing to do with the embedding model at all, such as an unrelated prompt change or model version update that happened around the same time.

My first step would be to run the retrieval-only evaluation, recall@k and precision@k against our labeled set of questions and known correct source chunks, comparing the old and new embedding models directly on that metric alone, holding every other part of the pipeline constant.

If retrieval metrics are roughly unchanged or even improved with the new embedding model, that strongly suggests the answer correctness drop is coming from the generation stage or some other pipeline change, not the embedding model, and I would then check faithfulness and answer relevance scores specifically, and audit whether anything else changed in the same deployment, such as a prompt template update or a different LLM version.

If retrieval metrics did in fact drop with the new embedding model, that confirms the regression is genuinely there, and I would investigate further, checking whether it's specific to certain query types (exact-term queries, multi-hop questions) rather than assuming a uniform quality drop, since that would point toward complementary fixes like hybrid search rather than reverting the embedding model outright.
hints: Refuse to conclude the embedding model is at fault from the end-to-end metric alone.
Isolate retrieval quality specifically (recall@k, precision@k) before attributing the regression to any one component.
Check for confounding changes (prompt, model version) that shipped alongside the embedding model swap.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.explanation: recall_at_k isolates retrieval quality alone, independent of anything the LLM generates, while faithfulness_score isolates generation quality given a fixed context, using an LLM judge to check whether the answer actually stays grounded in that context; running both separately is what lets you attribute a quality change to the correct pipeline stage.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Evaluating a RAG system with only one end-to-end 'is the final answer correct' metric, and drawing conclusions about which specific component (embedding model, chunking, prompt, reranker) to blame or credit for a change in that single number.
blocks.whyItHappens: An end-to-end metric is the simplest thing to compute and matches what users actually experience, so it's tempting to treat it as sufficient without building the additional labeled evaluation data needed to isolate retrieval from generation.
blocks.correctApproach: Maintain a labeled evaluation set with known correct source chunks and reference answers, and compute retrieval metrics (recall@k, precision@k) and generation metrics (faithfulness, answer relevance) separately so any pipeline change can be attributed to the stage it actually affected.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: Maintain a labeled evaluation set covering realistic query diversity, measure retrieval and generation quality as separate metrics on every meaningful pipeline change, and periodically validate any LLM-as-judge metric against real human review to catch judge-model blind spots.
keyPoints: Keep a labeled evaluation set with known correct source chunks and reference answers, covering realistic query diversity.
Always compute retrieval metrics (recall@k, precision@k, MRR) separately from generation metrics (faithfulness, answer relevance).
Periodically validate LLM-as-judge scoring against real human review rather than trusting it unconditionally.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: What's the difference between faithfulness and answer relevance as evaluation metrics?
blocks.answer: Faithfulness measures whether the generated answer is actually supported by and consistent with the retrieved context, catching cases where the model adds unsupported claims or contradicts its own source material, while answer relevance measures whether the answer actually addresses the user's question, which are independent properties: an answer can be perfectly faithful to the context yet fail to actually answer what was asked, or vice versa.

title: What Is an AI Agent
description: An AI agent is a model wrapped in a loop that can choose actions, call tools and observe results across multiple steps instead of answering in a single pass.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

A plain LLM call is a single forward pass: prompt in, completion out, done. An agent wraps that same model in a loop where each iteration the model can decide to call a tool, read the tool's output, and decide again, until it judges the task finished or a stop condition is hit. The 'agent' behavior is not a different model, it is the control loop and the tool contracts around it.

Why this matters

Many real tasks cannot be solved in one shot because the information needed to answer only becomes available after taking an action, such as querying a database, running code, or searching the web. Wrapping a model in a loop with tools turns a static text predictor into something that can gather evidence and correct course, but it also introduces new failure modes: infinite loops, compounding tool errors, and runaway cost from every extra step being another paid model call.

How it works

The orchestrator sends the model a system prompt describing the goal and the available tools (usually as JSON schemas), plus conversation history. The model returns either a final answer or a structured tool call. The orchestrator executes that tool call against real code, appends the tool's result back into the context as an observation, and calls the model again. This repeats until the model emits a final answer, a max-step budget is hit, or a guard rejects the plan. State (the accumulating transcript) is the only thing that makes it feel like the agent 'remembers' what happened.

When to use it

the task genuinely needs multiple dependent steps, external data the model does not have, or actions with side effects (booking, writing files, calling APIs), and a single prompt cannot supply all the needed context up front.

When not to use it

the task is answerable from the prompt and the model's own knowledge in one pass; adding a loop only adds latency, cost and new failure surface for no behavioral gain.
keyPoints: An agent is a model plus a loop plus tools, not a fundamentally different model.
The loop lets the model gather evidence and revise a plan instead of guessing everything up front.
Each step is a full model call: the transcript of prompts, tool calls and observations is the only memory.
Best fit: multi-step tasks needing external data or actions with real side effects.
Avoid when: a single prompt already contains everything needed to answer correctly.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Your product manager wants to turn a working single-prompt 'summarize this ticket' feature into an 'agent' that also files the ticket, pings the right Slack channel and updates a spreadsheet. How do you scope this without over-engineering it?
blocks.answer:
I would first separate what genuinely needs a loop from what is just sequential automation. Summarizing is still one model call. Filing the ticket, pinging Slack and updating the spreadsheet are three deterministic side-effecting actions that could be scripted directly after the summary is produced, with no need for the model to decide the order or whether to retry.

The part that actually benefits from agent behavior is if the model needs to make a judgment call using the outputs of earlier steps, for example deciding which Slack channel based on ticket content it just read, or deciding whether the spreadsheet update requires deduplication after seeing existing rows. That is where I would give the model tool definitions for 'create_ticket', 'post_slack_message' and 'update_row', each with a narrow JSON schema, and let it choose the sequence and arguments based on what it observes.

I would cap the loop at a small number of steps (this task needs at most 3-4 tool calls), log every tool call and its arguments before executing, and make each tool idempotent or checked (e.g. check for an existing ticket before creating one) so a retried step does not create duplicates.

Finally I would keep a non-agentic fallback: if any tool call fails validation, stop the loop and hand off to a human with the partial state, rather than letting the model improvise around a tool error. Not every automation needs autonomy; the agent framing is only worth the cost where a judgment call actually depends on intermediate results.
hints: Distinguish steps that need model judgment from steps that are just deterministic automation.
Give the model narrow tool schemas and a hard step budget.
Make tools idempotent and add a human-handoff fallback on failure.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.code:
MAX_STEPS = 6

def run_agent(user_goal, tools, llm_call):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": user_goal}]
    for step in range(MAX_STEPS):
        response = llm_call(messages, tools=tools)
        if response.tool_call is None:
            return response.text  # model produced a final answer
        tool_result = execute_tool(response.tool_call, tools)
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "tool_call": response.tool_call})
        messages.append({"role": "tool", "content": tool_result})
    raise RuntimeError("Agent exceeded max steps without a final answer")
blocks.explanation: This is the minimal shape of an agent loop: the model either finishes or requests a tool, the orchestrator executes the tool and feeds the result back as an observation, and a hard step cap prevents an unbounded, unbounded-cost loop.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Describing an agent as 'an AI that can think and act on its own' without mentioning the loop, the tool contract, or how state is passed between steps.
blocks.whyItHappens: The marketing language around agents obscures that there is no new reasoning capability involved; interviewees repeat the vague framing instead of the concrete control-flow mechanism, because they have used agent products but not built the loop themselves.
blocks.correctApproach: Explain the concrete mechanism: the model returns either text or a structured tool call each turn, the orchestrator executes tools and appends observations to the transcript, and the loop terminates on a final answer, a step budget, or a guard condition.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: Every extra loop iteration is a full model call, so agents trade latency and cost for the ability to gather evidence and self-correct. The right scope is the smallest loop that still lets the model make the judgment calls a fixed script cannot.
keyPoints: Set a hard max-step budget and log every tool call before execution.
Prefer a deterministic script over an agent loop whenever the step order and arguments do not depend on intermediate results.
Test the loop's termination behavior explicitly: what happens on tool failure, ambiguous observations, and hitting the step cap.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: How is an agent different from a plain chatbot with function calling enabled?
blocks.answer: Function calling is the mechanism; an agent is the pattern of calling the model repeatedly in a loop, feeding tool results back in, until it decides it is done. A chatbot can use function calling for a single call-and-respond turn without ever looping autonomously.

title: The ReAct Pattern
description: ReAct interleaves reasoning traces with tool actions and their observations, letting the model adjust its plan based on what a tool actually returned.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

ReAct (Reason + Act) asks the model to explicitly interleave a short 'Thought' (reasoning about what to do next), an 'Action' (a tool call), and then receive an 'Observation' (the tool's real output) before producing the next Thought. Instead of planning everything up front, the model re-plans after every observation.

Why this matters

Without the explicit thought step, a tool-calling loop still works but the model's tool choices are less grounded and harder to debug, because you only see inputs and outputs, not the stated reason for a decision. The Thought text also acts as working memory that keeps the model anchored to the original goal across many tool calls, which matters because context windows and attention degrade over long transcripts.

How it works

The prompt template forces the format: 'Thought: ... Action: tool_name(args) Observation: <filled in by orchestrator> Thought: ...' repeated until the model emits 'Final Answer: ...'. The orchestrator parses the Action line, executes the real tool, and substitutes the Observation before the next model call. Because the reasoning is now text the model itself generated and can re-read, it self-corrects more reliably than a pattern that only sees raw tool JSON, especially when an early tool call returns something unexpected like an empty result or an error.

When to use it

multi-step lookup or research tasks where the next action genuinely depends on what the previous tool returned, and where visibility into the model's stated reasoning is valuable for debugging or auditing.

When not to use it

the task is a single deterministic tool call, or you are using a model API with native structured tool calling where the framework already handles the act/observe loop and forcing a verbose Thought format only adds tokens without adding grounding.
keyPoints: ReAct explicitly alternates Thought, Action and Observation instead of planning everything in one shot.
The written Thought is working memory that keeps the model anchored to the goal across a long transcript.
Implemented via a strict text format the orchestrator parses, executes, and re-injects as Observation.
Best fit: multi-step research or lookup tasks where the next action depends on the last tool result.
Avoid when: a single deterministic tool call suffices, or native structured tool calling already covers the loop.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: An agent built on the ReAct pattern is stuck calling the same search tool five times in a row with slightly reworded queries, never reaching a final answer. How do you diagnose and fix this?
blocks.answer:
I would first read the actual Thought/Action/Observation transcript rather than just the final failure, because ReAct's whole value is that the reasoning is visible. Usually this loop happens because the Observation returned is genuinely unhelpful (empty results, or results that don't address the sub-question), and the model's Thought keeps concluding 'I need to search again' without escalating.

The fix is rarely a smarter model; it is a better loop contract. I would add an explicit step counter and a rule such as 'if the same tool has been called more than twice for a similar query, you must either try a different tool or give a partial answer stating what is missing.' I would also inspect whether the search tool's result format is actually usable by the model, for example whether it's returning full page text versus useless metadata.

I would add a hard step budget with a graceful degradation path: at the step limit, force a final response that states the answer so far and what could not be confirmed, rather than letting the orchestrator throw an unhandled loop-exceeded error to the user.

Finally I would add this exact failure (repeated near-duplicate queries with no new information) as a regression case in my eval set, since it's a common enough agent failure mode that it will recur with other tools.
hints: Read the actual Thought/Action/Observation trace, not just the final output.
Add a repetition guard and a step budget with graceful degradation.
Check whether the tool's output format is actually usable by the model.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.code:
REACT_PROMPT = """Answer using this exact format:
Thought: reasoning about what to do next
Action: tool_name[input]
Observation: (filled in for you)
... repeat Thought/Action/Observation ...
Thought: I now know the final answer
Final Answer: the answer
"""

def parse_action(text):
    # naive parse of 'Action: tool_name[input]'
    line = [l for l in text.splitlines() if l.startswith("Action:")][0]
    name, arg = line[len("Action:"):].strip().split("[", 1)
    return name.strip(), arg.rstrip("]")
blocks.explanation: The strict Thought/Action/Observation format is what makes ReAct parseable and debuggable: the orchestrator only needs to extract the Action line, run the tool, and append the result as the next Observation before calling the model again.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Treating ReAct as just 'giving the model tools' and conflating it with any tool-calling agent, without mentioning the explicit reasoning trace or why it improves grounding.
blocks.whyItHappens: Modern model APIs handle structured tool calling natively, so the visible Thought text that defined the original ReAct paper is often abstracted away, and people who have only used framework-level agents never see the underlying pattern it's built on.
blocks.correctApproach: Name the specific mechanism: interleaved Thought/Action/Observation text that gives the model a re-readable record of its own reasoning, which is what improves multi-step grounding compared to a bare act-and-observe loop.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: Explicit reasoning traces improve grounding and debuggability but add tokens and latency to every step, since the model is generating extra text that costs money whether or not it changes the outcome.
keyPoints: Cap consecutive repeated actions and force escalation or graceful partial answers.
Log the Thought text; it is your primary debugging signal for agent misbehavior.
Measure whether the extra reasoning tokens actually change tool choice versus just adding cost, and drop the pattern if they don't.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: Is ReAct still relevant now that most model providers support native structured tool calling?
blocks.answer: The explicit text format is less necessary since native tool calling already returns structured actions and the framework manages observations, but the underlying idea, reason then act then re-plan on the real observation, is still exactly what production agent loops do under the hood.

title: Function and Tool Calling
description: Tool calling lets a model emit a structured request to invoke a named function with arguments, and the calling application executes it and returns the result for the model to continue with.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

You describe each available tool to the model as a JSON schema: a name, a description, and a parameters object with typed fields. When the model decides a tool is needed, instead of writing free text it emits a structured object matching that schema, for example {"name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Pune"}}. Your application code, not the model, actually executes the function and sends the result back.

Why this matters

Before structured tool calling, developers had to ask the model to output JSON in free text and hope it was parseable, which broke constantly on malformed brackets or extra prose. Providers now train models specifically to emit calls matching a given schema and to stop generation at the right point, which makes the argument extraction reliable enough to call real, side-effecting code, such as charging a card or sending an email, directly from model output.

How it works

The schema is passed alongside the prompt on every request. During decoding, the model is constrained or strongly biased toward producing valid JSON that matches one of the declared tool schemas when it chooses to call a tool; some providers use grammar-constrained decoding to guarantee schema validity, others rely on fine-tuning plus a validation retry. The app must still validate the returned arguments against the schema and against business rules before executing, because model output is untrusted input even when it is syntactically valid JSON.

When to use it

the model needs to trigger real actions, retrieve live data, or produce output your system will parse programmatically, and you can define a stable, narrow schema for that action.

When not to use it

the action has no clear discrete parameters, is purely about generating text, or the schema would need to be so broad that it stops constraining the model in any useful way.
keyPoints: Tools are declared as JSON schemas; the model emits structured arguments, and your code executes the real function.
Native tool calling replaced fragile 'ask the model to output parseable JSON' prompting.
Providers use fine-tuning and/or constrained decoding to make schema-valid output reliable, but never guaranteed safe.
Best fit: triggering real side-effecting actions or structured retrieval with a narrow, well-defined schema.
Avoid when: the action isn't decomposable into stable typed parameters, or free text is genuinely the right output.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: A support-bot agent has a 'refund_order' tool. In testing, the model occasionally calls it with an order ID that doesn't belong to the current user, apparently hallucinated from context. How do you prevent this in production?
blocks.answer:
I would treat the model's tool call arguments as untrusted input from an unauthenticated source, exactly like a request body from the public internet, regardless of how confident the JSON looks. The schema validation that tool calling gives you only guarantees shape and types, not business correctness.

Concretely, I would never let the model supply the order ID as a free identifier tied to money movement. Instead I'd scope the tool so the order ID is resolved server-side from the authenticated session (e.g. 'refund current user's most recent order' or a tool that first lists only that user's orders, and the model must choose from that returned list), removing the possibility of an arbitrary or hallucinated ID being accepted.

Where an arbitrary ID genuinely has to be passed, I would add a server-side authorization check that the order belongs to the requesting user before executing the refund, independent of anything the model asserted, and I'd cap refund amount and frequency with hard business rules that don't trust model judgment for financial limits.

Finally, I would log every tool call with its arguments and the authorization decision, and add this exact case, a plausible-looking but wrong ID, to my eval set so a future prompt or model change doesn't silently reopen the hole.
hints: Treat tool-call arguments as untrusted input regardless of schema validity.
Scope tools so sensitive identifiers are resolved server-side, not supplied by the model.
Enforce business authorization and limits independent of the model's stated intent.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.explanation: A narrow tool schema with required fields and additionalProperties set to false limits what the model can pass, but note the schema alone does not verify that order_id actually belongs to the caller; that check has to happen in application code after the call is received.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Saying 'the model calls the function' as if the model executes code, without distinguishing that the model only emits a structured request which the application must validate and execute.
blocks.whyItHappens: The API terminology ('function calling', 'tool use') and demo code that directly maps tool_call.name to a Python dict of functions makes it easy to blur the line between 'the model decided' and 'the model executed', especially when no validation layer is shown in tutorials.
blocks.correctApproach: State plainly that the model only proposes a call; your code is the one that validates arguments against the schema and business rules, executes the function, and decides whether the result is safe to return, exactly as you would for any other untrusted client input.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: Tool calling makes model output actionable, which is exactly why it needs the same input validation, authorization and rate limiting you'd apply to any external API caller; more tools also means more schema for the model to choose between, which can degrade selection accuracy.
keyPoints: Validate tool arguments against both schema and business rules before execution, every time.
Keep each tool schema narrow and single-purpose; broad multi-mode tools increase misuse and misselection.
Test with adversarial and malformed arguments, not just the happy path the model usually produces.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: What happens if you give a model 40 tools instead of 5?
blocks.answer: Selection accuracy typically degrades because the model has to disambiguate between more overlapping schemas and descriptions within the same context; in practice teams group tools by task, dynamically filter which tools are exposed per request, or use a router step to narrow the set before the main call.

title: Multi-Agent Systems
description: Multi-agent systems split a task across specialized agents, such as a planner and several workers, which improves focus per agent but adds coordination and failure-handling overhead.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

Instead of one agent with a huge system prompt and every tool, you split the work: an orchestrator/planner agent decomposes the task and delegates sub-tasks to specialized worker agents (a researcher, a coder, a reviewer), each with its own focused prompt, tools and often a different underlying model sized to its sub-task.

Why this matters

A single agent juggling too many tools and instructions suffers from prompt dilution: instructions for one sub-task interfere with instructions for another, and the model has to hold the entire task's context at once. Splitting into specialized agents keeps each one's context small and its tool set unambiguous, which measurably improves reliability on complex tasks, but every hop between agents is a serialization point where information can be lost, misinterpreted or duplicated, and debugging now spans multiple transcripts instead of one.

How it works

The most common topology is orchestrator-worker: a planner agent produces a task list or a single delegated instruction, calls a worker agent as if it were a tool (passing it a scoped sub-task and only the context it needs), receives the worker's result, and either continues delegating or synthesizes a final answer. Communication between agents is usually just text or structured JSON passed through the orchestrator, not a shared memory space, so each agent only knows what it was explicitly told.

When to use it

the task decomposes cleanly into independent or loosely-coupled sub-tasks, different sub-tasks benefit from different tools, prompts or models, or a single agent's context and instructions are becoming unmanageable and error-prone.

When not to use it

the task is small enough for one focused agent, or the sub-tasks are so tightly coupled that coordination overhead and error compounding across agents would cost more than the isolation benefit.
keyPoints: Multi-agent systems delegate sub-tasks to specialized agents instead of overloading one agent's prompt and tool set.
The common orchestrator-worker topology treats worker agents like callable tools with scoped context.
Specialization reduces prompt dilution but adds serialization points where information can be lost between agents.
Best fit: cleanly decomposable tasks, or a single agent whose instructions/tools have become unmanageable.
Avoid when: the task is small or sub-tasks are too tightly coupled for delegation overhead to pay off.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: You built a 3-agent pipeline (researcher, writer, editor) for a content-generation product. Quality is good but latency and cost tripled compared to the single-agent version, and stakeholders want to know if the multi-agent design is worth it. How do you evaluate that?
blocks.answer:
I would first quantify what the split actually bought versus its cost: run the same eval set through both the single-agent and multi-agent pipelines, comparing an actual quality metric, not just a vibe check, against latency and token cost per request. If the multi-agent version isn't meaningfully better on the metric that matters for the product, the added cost isn't justified regardless of how it looks in a demo.

If quality genuinely improved, I would look for where the gain came from: often it is one specific hop, such as the editor agent catching factual errors the writer introduced, that provides most of the value, while the other split (researcher vs writer) contributes less. I'd try collapsing the low-value split back into one agent to see if quality holds, which usually cuts cost significantly without losing much.

For the hops that stay separate, I'd reduce cost by using a cheaper, faster model for lower-stakes sub-tasks (like initial research) and reserving the strongest model for the sub-task that most affects final quality (like editing), rather than running all three agents on the same expensive model.

Finally I would present the trade-off explicitly to stakeholders in terms of cost-per-quality-point-gained, not architecture preference, since the honest answer might be that the added coordination overhead isn't worth it for this product's margins even if it produces marginally better output.
hints: Measure quality delta against cost/latency delta on a real eval set, not intuition.
Identify which specific agent hop actually drives the quality gain.
Right-size the model per sub-task instead of running everything on the most expensive model.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.explanation: The orchestrator decomposes the task and calls each worker with a narrowly scoped instruction and only the context that sub-task needs, then synthesizes the final answer from the collected worker results, keeping each worker's context small and focused.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Reaching for a multi-agent architecture by default because it 'sounds more sophisticated', without measuring whether it beats a single well-scoped agent on the actual task.
blocks.whyItHappens: Multi-agent frameworks are heavily marketed and demoed on impressive-looking complex tasks, so it's tempting to assume more agents equals more capability, without accounting for the coordination overhead, extra latency, and new failure modes (lost context between agents, error compounding) that scale with the number of hops.
blocks.correctApproach: Start with the smallest single-agent design that could work, and only split into multiple agents when you can point to a specific reason a single agent's context or tool set is causing measurable failures, then validate the split actually improves the metric that matters.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: Specialization improves per-agent reliability but multiplies latency, cost and the number of places a task can silently go wrong; every inter-agent handoff needs the same scrutiny as an API contract between services.
keyPoints: A/B the multi-agent pipeline against a strong single-agent baseline on the same eval set before committing to it.
Right-size the model per agent role instead of defaulting every agent to the most capable (and expensive) model.
Log and trace every inter-agent handoff so failures can be attributed to a specific agent, not just the pipeline as a whole.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: How do you prevent two agents from disagreeing and looping forever, e.g. a writer and a critic that never converge?
blocks.answer: Cap the number of critique/revision rounds explicitly, require the critic to produce a bounded, actionable list of issues rather than open-ended feedback, and force a final decision (accept or escalate to a human) once the round limit is hit rather than letting the exchange continue indefinitely.

title: Agent Memory and the Model Context Protocol
description: Agent memory persists useful state across turns or sessions, and protocols like MCP standardize how an agent discovers and calls external tools and data sources.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

An LLM has no memory between separate API calls; every call is stateless. 'Agent memory' is an engineering layer built on top: short-term memory is just the growing conversation transcript passed back in each call, while long-term memory is information deliberately extracted, summarized or embedded and stored outside the context window (a database, a vector store), then selectively retrieved and re-injected into future prompts. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a separate concern: an open, standardized protocol for how an agent/client discovers and invokes tools, resources and prompts exposed by external servers, so you don't have to write a bespoke integration for every tool provider.

Why this matters

Without an explicit memory strategy, a long-running agent either forgets everything each session (bad for personalization or ongoing tasks) or keeps stuffing the growing raw transcript into every call (bad for cost and eventually exceeds the context window, and quality degrades on very long contexts even before the hard limit). Without a standard like MCP, every new tool integration is bespoke glue code, and switching agent frameworks means rewriting all your tool adapters from scratch.

How it works

Short-term memory is managed by truncating, summarizing or windowing the transcript once it grows past a budget. Long-term memory typically stores facts as embeddings in a vector database or as structured key-value records, retrieved by similarity or by explicit lookup and injected as a compact block into the next prompt, rather than replaying the entire history. MCP defines a client-server model over JSON-RPC: an MCP server exposes 'tools' (callable functions with schemas), 'resources' (readable data) and 'prompts', and an MCP client (the agent host) discovers what's available at connection time and calls them using the standard protocol, meaning the same MCP server (e.g. a GitHub or Postgres integration) can be plugged into any MCP-compatible agent without custom code.

When to use it

long-term memory: when a user or task genuinely benefits from recalling information across sessions (preferences, prior decisions, ongoing project state). MCP: when you want tool integrations that are reusable across agents/products rather than hardcoded to one app's internal tool-calling code.

When not to use it

long-term memory: for short single-session tasks where replaying the transcript is cheap and simpler, since added memory is also added attack surface for stale or leaked information. MCP: for a single internal tool used by exactly one agent, where the protocol overhead isn't worth it over a direct function call.
keyPoints: LLM calls are stateless; short-term memory is the replayed transcript, long-term memory is deliberately extracted and re-retrieved state.
MCP standardizes tool/resource/prompt discovery and invocation between agent hosts and external servers via JSON-RPC.
Long-term memory usually means embedding or structuring facts for retrieval, not replaying raw history.
Best fit for memory: multi-session tasks needing recall; best fit for MCP: tool integrations meant to be reused across agents.
Avoid when: short single-session tasks (skip long-term memory) or a single bespoke internal tool (skip the protocol overhead).

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Users complain your AI assistant 'forgets' preferences they stated three sessions ago, but you're also worried about unbounded storage growth and about the assistant recalling something a user explicitly asked it to forget. How do you design the memory layer?
blocks.answer:
I would separate what actually needs to persist from what is just conversational noise. Not every statement in a session deserves long-term storage; I'd run a lightweight extraction step, either at end of session or periodically, that pulls out explicit, durable facts (stated preferences, ongoing project details) into structured records rather than storing raw transcripts wholesale, which controls storage growth and keeps retrieval precise.

For recall, I would retrieve only the small set of memory records relevant to the current query, typically via embedding similarity plus recency/importance weighting, and inject just that compact summary into the prompt rather than replaying old sessions verbatim, since bloating every new prompt with all historical memory increases cost and can actually dilute the model's focus on the current request.

For forgetting, I would build an explicit deletion path: a user command like 'forget that' should hard-delete the specific memory record, not just suppress it in the prompt, since a soft-suppressed but still-stored fact is a data-handling liability if it surfaces later through a bug, an export request, or a different retrieval path. I would also expose stored memories to the user so they can audit and delete them directly, treating this as a privacy feature, not just a UX nicety.

Finally I would put a TTL or periodic review on stored memories, since 'true a year ago' isn't always true now, and add tests that confirm a deleted memory never resurfaces via retrieval, caching or backups.
hints: Extract durable structured facts instead of storing or replaying raw transcripts.
Retrieve only relevant memory per query rather than injecting full history.
Make forgetting a real hard-delete, auditable and tested, not a soft suppression.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.explanation: This is the shape of an MCP client request: a standard JSON-RPC call to invoke a named tool exposed by an MCP server, with arguments matching that tool's declared schema, regardless of which agent framework is making the call.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Describing agent memory as 'the model remembers things' or describing MCP as 'a way for AI to use tools' without explaining the actual storage/retrieval mechanism or the client-server protocol structure.
blocks.whyItHappens: Both concepts are usually experienced through a polished product surface (a chat app that 'just remembers', an IDE that 'just has tools'), so the underlying mechanics, stateless calls plus explicit retrieval, or JSON-RPC tool discovery, are invisible unless you've built or debugged the integration yourself.
blocks.correctApproach: Explain memory as an explicit extract-store-retrieve-inject pipeline built outside the stateless model call, and explain MCP as a standard client-server protocol for tool/resource discovery and invocation, distinct from any single vendor's proprietary tool-calling format.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: Memory improves personalization and continuity but adds a real data-handling surface with privacy and staleness risk; MCP improves tool reusability and reduces integration glue but adds a protocol layer that's unnecessary for a single bespoke internal tool.
keyPoints: Store structured, extracted facts with provenance and TTLs, not raw transcript dumps.
Build and test a genuine hard-delete path for memory, since 'forget' has to mean actually deleted.
Adopt MCP when a tool integration needs to be reused across agents or products, not for a single internal call site.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: How is MCP different from just calling a REST API directly from your agent code?
blocks.answer: MCP standardizes discovery (the agent can enumerate what tools/resources a server offers and their schemas at connection time) and invocation format across any MCP-compatible server, so the same integration works across different agent hosts without bespoke glue code, whereas a direct REST call is a one-off integration specific to that agent's codebase.
