title: Fine-Tuning vs Prompting vs RAG
description: Prompting changes behavior instantly with no training, RAG adds fresh or private knowledge at query time, and fine-tuning bakes a skill or style into the weights themselves.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

All three change what an LLM effectively 'knows' or does for your task, but at different points and with different costs. Prompting changes behavior through the instructions and examples you put in the context window at request time; nothing about the model changes. RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) fetches relevant documents at query time and inserts them into the context so the model can ground its answer in facts it wasn't trained on. Fine-tuning actually updates the model's weights on your own examples, so the behavior is baked in and no longer depends on what's in the prompt.

Why this matters

Picking the wrong one wastes money and doesn't fix the actual problem. If your issue is the model doesn't know today's data or your private documents, fine-tuning barely helps and goes stale immediately; RAG is the fix. If your issue is the model doesn't consistently follow a format, tone or a narrow skill even with a good prompt and good examples in context, that's when fine-tuning earns its cost, since it changes the model's default behavior instead of relying on it to obey instructions correctly every time. If the issue is just that the model needs better instructions or examples, prompting is by far the cheapest fix and should always be tried and exhausted first.

How it works

Prompting: system + user messages plus few-shot examples, no infra beyond your existing API calls. RAG: an offline indexing pipeline chunks and embeds your documents into a vector store, and an online retrieval step embeds the query, finds nearest chunks, and inserts them into the prompt before generation. Fine-tuning: you assemble a labeled dataset of input/output pairs reflecting the desired behavior, then run a training job (full fine-tune or a parameter-efficient method) that adjusts weights via gradient descent on that dataset, producing a new model checkpoint you deploy and pay to host or call.

When to use it

prompting for instruction-following and formatting issues fixable with better wording or few-shot examples; RAG when the model needs current, private or large amounts of factual context it can't memorize; fine-tuning when you need consistent behavior, a specific style/format at scale, or domain adaptation that a prompt can't reliably enforce.

When not to use it

don't reach for fine-tuning to fix a knowledge gap (use RAG instead, since fine-tuned facts still get stale and are hard to update); don't reach for RAG to fix a formatting or tone problem prompting could solve; don't fine-tune before you've exhausted prompting, since fine-tuning is the most expensive, slowest-to-iterate option of the three.
keyPoints: Prompting changes behavior via context at request time; RAG injects retrieved facts at request time; fine-tuning updates the model's weights permanently.
Use RAG for knowledge gaps and freshness, fine-tuning for consistent skill/style/format, prompting for instruction-following issues.
Fine-tuning is the most expensive and slowest to iterate; always exhaust prompting first.
Best fit: match the technique to the actual failure mode (knowledge vs behavior vs instruction-following), and they compose (RAG + a fine-tuned model is common).
Avoid when: fine-tuning to patch a knowledge gap that goes stale immediately, or RAG to fix a pure formatting/tone problem.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: A team wants to fine-tune a model on their internal wiki so the assistant 'knows the company's policies'. They've budgeted for a training run. How do you respond?
blocks.answer:
I would push back on the plan before the budget is spent, because fine-tuning is usually the wrong tool for 'knowing' a body of documents. Fine-tuning bakes patterns from training examples into weights; it doesn't reliably memorize a document corpus verbatim, and any policy that changes next quarter would require re-training to stay accurate, which is expensive and slow.

What they actually want is RAG: index the wiki into a vector store, retrieve the relevant sections for each user question, and put them in context so the model answers grounded in the actual current text, with a citation back to the source page. This also gives them something fine-tuning can't: when policy changes, you just re-index the changed page, not retrain a model.

If, separately, the assistant's tone or the way it phrases policy answers is inconsistent or doesn't match the desired style even with a good prompt, that's a legitimate reason to consider fine-tuning on top of RAG, for the response style rather than for the facts, so the model always answers in the same format after retrieving grounded context.

I would recommend they build the RAG pipeline first, measure quality with a small eval set of real policy questions, and only revisit fine-tuning if a specific, prompt-resistant behavior problem remains after RAG is working, since that keeps the expensive option as a last resort rather than a first guess.
hints: Recognize this is a knowledge-freshness problem, which RAG solves and fine-tuning does not.
Explain why fine-tuning goes stale and is costly to update versus re-indexing documents.
Note that fine-tuning could still be justified separately for style/format, on top of RAG.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.code:
def answer(query, vector_store, llm_call):
    # RAG: retrieve first, then generate grounded in retrieved chunks
    chunks = vector_store.similarity_search(query, k=4)
    context = "\n\n".join(c.text for c in chunks)
    prompt = f"Answer using only this context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {query}"
    return llm_call(prompt)
# Contrast: fine-tuning changes llm_call's underlying weights, not this per-request code.
blocks.explanation: RAG's cost lives in the retrieval step and the per-request prompt construction; nothing about the model itself changes, which is exactly why updating the knowledge source is as cheap as re-indexing a document rather than retraining.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Recommending fine-tuning as the default 'more advanced/better' option whenever prompting isn't perfect, without diagnosing whether the failure is actually a knowledge gap, a style gap, or just a prompting gap.
blocks.whyItHappens: Fine-tuning sounds like the 'real' machine learning solution compared to 'just writing a better prompt', so it's tempting to reach for it as a status upgrade rather than diagnosing which of the three failure modes is actually present.
blocks.correctApproach: Diagnose first: is the model missing facts (RAG), missing consistent behavior/format despite a good prompt (fine-tuning), or just under-instructed (better prompting)? Only fine-tune once prompting and RAG have been tried and a specific behavior gap remains.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: The three techniques compose rather than compete: many production systems use RAG for facts, a lightly fine-tuned model for consistent format/tone, and careful prompting for instructions, choosing the cheapest technique that fixes the specific observed failure.
keyPoints: Exhaust prompting and RAG before considering fine-tuning; fine-tuning is the slowest and most expensive to iterate on.
Re-evaluate RAG retrieval quality and prompt wording before blaming 'the model' for a wrong answer.
Track which technique fixed which failure in your eval set so future regressions are diagnosed quickly.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: Can you combine RAG and fine-tuning in the same system?
blocks.answer: Yes, and it's common: fine-tune the model to reliably follow a specific answer format, citation style, or domain reasoning pattern, while still using RAG to supply the current, factual context the fine-tuned model reasons over at request time.

title: LoRA and Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
description: LoRA and other PEFT methods train a small number of additional low-rank parameters instead of the whole model, making customization far cheaper and easier to swap per use case.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

Full fine-tuning updates every weight in the model, which for a multi-billion parameter model means storing and computing gradients for billions of numbers, needing enormous GPU memory. LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) instead freezes the original weights entirely and injects small trainable low-rank matrices (A and B, where the update is approximated as a product of two much smaller matrices) alongside specific layers, typically the attention projections. Only those low-rank matrices, a tiny fraction of the total parameter count, get trained.

Why this matters

Because the base weights never change, you can fine-tune on consumer-grade or modest cloud GPUs instead of a multi-GPU cluster, training finishes in a fraction of the time, and the resulting artifact (the LoRA 'adapter') is often only tens of megabytes instead of tens of gigabytes. That means you can maintain many task-specific or customer-specific adapters cheaply and swap them at inference time on top of the same shared base model, rather than hosting a full separate model per customization.

How it works

For a frozen weight matrix W, LoRA adds a delta ΔW = B·A where A and B are much lower rank (dimension r, typically 4-64) than W. During training, only A and B receive gradient updates; W stays frozen. At inference, the effective weight is W + B·A, computed either by merging the adapter into a copy of the base weights or by adding the low-rank term on the fly. QLoRA extends this further by quantizing the frozen base weights to 4-bit precision to cut memory even more while keeping the trainable adapter in higher precision.

When to use it

you need to customize a specific behavior, tone, domain vocabulary or narrow skill without the cost of full fine-tuning, especially when you need multiple different customizations of the same base model (per customer, per task) that must be swappable and cheap to store.

When not to use it

the target behavior requires such a large distributional shift from the base model's capabilities that low-rank updates can't capture it (rare, but possible for very different domains or languages the base model has almost no exposure to), in which case full fine-tuning or continued pretraining may be necessary instead.
keyPoints: LoRA freezes the base model and trains small low-rank matrices injected into specific layers instead of all weights.
This cuts GPU memory and training time dramatically and produces tiny, swappable adapter files.
The effective weight at inference is the frozen base plus the low-rank product B·A; QLoRA also quantizes the frozen base to 4-bit.
Best fit: customizing style/domain/skill cheaply, especially with many swappable per-customer or per-task adapters.
Avoid when: the needed shift is too large for a low-rank update to represent, warranting full fine-tuning instead.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: You need to offer 50 enterprise customers a version of your assistant fine-tuned on each customer's own support tone and terminology, but hosting 50 full fine-tuned models is clearly not viable on your infra budget. How would you architect this?
blocks.answer:
I would use LoRA specifically because the problem is 'many small, swappable customizations of the same base capability', which is exactly what low-rank adapters are designed for. I'd train one lightweight adapter per customer on their own historical support transcripts, keeping the shared base model frozen and identical across all customers.

At serving time, I would host a single copy of the base model and dynamically load or apply the relevant customer's adapter per request, either by merging weights on the fly for that request's batch or by using a serving framework that supports multiple concurrent LoRA adapters against one base model. This avoids the GPU memory cost of 50 separate full models, since each adapter is a small fraction of the base model's size.

I would still validate each customer's adapter against a held-out eval set of that customer's real support scenarios before shipping it, since a badly curated training set can make an adapter overfit to a narrow tone and generalize poorly to novel questions. I'd also version each adapter alongside the base model version it was trained against, since an adapter trained against one base checkpoint may not transfer cleanly to a newer one.

Finally I would keep a fallback: if an adapter degrades quality relative to the plain base model on some inputs, detected via ongoing evaluation, I would be able to disable that specific adapter and fall back to the base model without affecting other customers.
hints: Recognize this as a many-small-customizations problem that LoRA is designed for.
Explain how adapters are swapped or applied per request on top of a single shared base model.
Cover per-customer validation, versioning against the base model, and a fallback path.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.code:
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model

config = LoraConfig(
    r=16,                # rank of the low-rank matrices
    lora_alpha=32,        # scaling factor for the update
    target_modules=["q_proj", "v_proj"],  # inject only into attention projections
    lora_dropout=0.05,
    task_type="CAUSAL_LM",
)
model = get_peft_model(base_model, config)
model.print_trainable_parameters()  # typically well under 1% of total params
blocks.explanation: The base_model's original weights stay frozen; get_peft_model wraps it with trainable low-rank adapters only on the targeted attention projection layers, which is why print_trainable_parameters shows such a small fraction of parameters actually being trained.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Describing LoRA as just 'a faster way to fine-tune' without explaining the low-rank decomposition mechanism (freezing W, training B·A) or why that specifically reduces memory and enables adapter swapping.
blocks.whyItHappens: LoRA is usually encountered through a library call (get_peft_model) that hides the math, so people repeat 'it's cheaper' as a fact without being able to explain why freezing the base weights and training a low-rank delta is what produces both the memory savings and the small, portable adapter file.
blocks.correctApproach: Explain the actual decomposition: the base weight matrix is frozen, a low-rank delta B·A is trained on top of specific layers, gradients only flow through the small A and B matrices, and the resulting adapter is small enough to store and swap independently of the base model.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: Lower rank (r) means cheaper training and smaller adapters but less capacity to capture complex behavior changes; picking which layers to target and the right rank is itself an empirical tuning step, not a fixed default.
keyPoints: Start with a modest rank and expand only if the adapter underfits the target behavior on your eval set.
Version adapters against the exact base model checkpoint they were trained on.
Evaluate each adapter against both its target behavior and a general capability set to catch regressions from overfitting.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: What's the difference between LoRA and QLoRA?
blocks.answer: QLoRA additionally quantizes the frozen base model's weights to 4-bit precision before training, which drastically cuts the memory needed to even load the base model, while the trainable LoRA adapter itself is still kept and updated in higher precision.

title: RLHF and Alignment
description: Reinforcement learning from human feedback trains a model to prefer the responses humans rate as better, which is how raw next-token predictors become helpful, instruction-following assistants.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

A base pretrained model only learns to predict the next token over internet-scale text; it has no built-in notion of 'be helpful, follow instructions, refuse harmful requests'. RLHF adds that on top in stages: first supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on human-written example conversations to teach basic instruction-following, then training a separate reward model on human preference judgments (given two candidate responses, which is better), then using that reward model as a proxy reward signal to further tune the assistant model via reinforcement learning (commonly PPO, or more recent techniques like DPO which skip the explicit RL step).

Why this matters

This is literally the step that turns a raw autocomplete engine into a usable assistant, and it is also where most of a model's safety behavior, refusals, tone and helpfulness trade-offs get shaped, not from the pretraining data alone. Understanding RLHF matters for interviews because it explains real observed behaviors: why models sometimes give an overly hedged or overly agreeable answer (reward models can over-reward agreeableness or verbosity, a failure mode called reward hacking), and why 'jailbreaks' work at all (the safety behavior is a learned preference, not a hard rule, so a sufficiently unusual prompt can push the model outside the distribution the reward model was calibrated on).

How it works

Human labelers compare pairs of model outputs for the same prompt and rank which is preferred; this preference data trains a reward model to predict a scalar score matching human preference. The assistant model is then optimized to maximize that reward model's score on new prompts, typically with a KL-divergence penalty against the original SFT model so it doesn't drift too far and degenerate into reward-hacking gibberish that scores well but reads badly. DPO (Direct Preference Optimization) reformulates this as a direct classification loss over preference pairs, achieving a similar effect without training a separate reward model or running full RL.

When to use it

you're building or evaluating a general-purpose assistant where 'helpfulness' and 'safety behavior' need to be shaped from preference data rather than hardcoded rules, or you need to explain why a foundation model behaves the way it does in an interview or design discussion.

When not to use it

for narrow, deterministic tasks (classification, extraction) where hardcoded rules or simple supervised fine-tuning on labeled examples achieves the goal more reliably and cheaply than a full preference-based RL pipeline.
keyPoints: RLHF stages: supervised fine-tuning, then a reward model trained on human preference comparisons, then RL (or DPO) to optimize the assistant against that reward signal.
This is the step that adds helpfulness, instruction-following and most safety behavior on top of raw next-token prediction.
Reward hacking (over-optimizing for what the reward model rewards rather than what humans actually want) is a real, observable failure mode.
Best fit: explaining or shaping general-purpose assistant behavior and safety trade-offs.
Avoid when: a narrow deterministic task is better solved with simple supervised fine-tuning or rules.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Your team notices the assistant has become noticeably more verbose and sycophantic after a round of preference-data-driven fine-tuning, agreeing with users even when they're factually wrong. How do you explain and address this?
blocks.answer:
I would name this precisely as reward hacking: the reward model, trained on human preference comparisons, likely over-rewarded responses that are agreeable, long, or superficially thorough, because human labelers, even carefully instructed ones, tend to rate confident-sounding and agreeable answers higher on average, especially when comparing quickly. The assistant model then over-optimized against that biased signal rather than against 'actually correct and appropriately concise'.

To diagnose this, I would look at the preference data collection process itself: were labelers given clear criteria that penalize sycophancy and reward correctness even when it contradicts the user, or were they just asked which response they 'preferred' in a way that implicitly rewards agreeableness? I'd also check whether the KL penalty against the base SFT model during RL was strong enough, since too little constraint lets the policy drift further toward whatever the reward model over-rewards.

The fix is upstream, not a prompt patch: recollect or re-weight preference data with explicit instructions to penalize confident-but-wrong and unnecessarily agreeable responses, and consider adding a factuality or calibration signal directly into the reward model, not just holistic preference, since holistic human preference alone under-penalizes subtle correctness issues.

As a stop-gap while the training fix is in progress, I would add a lighter-weight mitigation at the application layer, like a system prompt instruction to disagree with incorrect factual claims and a post-hoc check, but I'd be explicit with the team that this treats the symptom; the actual fix requires correcting the reward signal, not layering more prompt instructions on top of a model that was optimized against a flawed proxy.
hints: Name the failure mode precisely: reward hacking from a biased or incomplete preference signal.
Diagnose whether labeler instructions and the RL KL constraint contributed to the drift.
Distinguish a real fix (better preference data/reward model) from a prompt-level stop-gap.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.code:
# Simplified DPO-style loss: push the policy to prefer 'chosen' over 'rejected'
# relative to a frozen reference model, without training a separate reward model.
import torch.nn.functional as F

def dpo_loss(policy_logp_chosen, policy_logp_rejected,
             ref_logp_chosen, ref_logp_rejected, beta=0.1):
    policy_diff = policy_logp_chosen - policy_logp_rejected
    ref_diff = ref_logp_chosen - ref_logp_rejected
    return -F.logsigmoid(beta * (policy_diff - ref_diff)).mean()
blocks.explanation: DPO turns the preference-optimization problem into a direct classification-style loss comparing how much more the policy (versus a frozen reference model) prefers the chosen response over the rejected one, avoiding the need to train and sample from a separate reward model during RL.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Saying 'RLHF makes the model safe' or 'RLHF makes the model good' as a black box, without describing the reward model, the preference data, or the reward-hacking failure mode that explains observed quirks like sycophancy.
blocks.whyItHappens: RLHF is usually summarized in one sentence in popular explanations ('trained with human feedback'), so the actual pipeline, SFT then reward model then RL/DPO, and its known failure modes get skipped, leaving no way to explain why specific weird behaviors happen.
blocks.correctApproach: Walk through the actual stages (SFT, reward model from preference comparisons, RL or DPO against that signal with a divergence constraint) and connect a specific observed behavior, like sycophancy or hedging, to a specific point in that pipeline where the signal was biased or under-constrained.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: RLHF/DPO meaningfully improves helpfulness and safety behavior over a raw pretrained model, but it optimizes against a learned proxy for human preference, not against ground truth, so it always carries some risk of reward hacking that has to be caught with targeted evals, not assumed away.
keyPoints: Evaluate for specific known failure modes (sycophancy, verbosity bias, overconfidence) with targeted test sets, not just general helpfulness scores.
Scrutinize preference-data collection instructions; vague 'which is better' labeling under-penalizes subtle correctness issues.
Keep a KL/divergence constraint against a trusted reference model during RL to limit drift into reward-hacked behavior.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: Why do some newer approaches use DPO instead of PPO-based RLHF?
blocks.answer: DPO reformulates preference optimization as a direct classification loss over chosen/rejected pairs relative to a reference model, avoiding the need to train a separate reward model and run unstable, sample-inefficient RL, which makes it simpler to implement and tune while achieving comparable alignment results in practice.

title: Distillation and Smaller Models
description: Distillation trains a smaller student model to mimic a larger teacher model's outputs, recovering much of the capability at a fraction of the inference cost.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

Distillation trains a smaller 'student' model to reproduce what a larger, more capable 'teacher' model would produce, rather than training the student from scratch on raw labeled data alone. In LLMs this is most commonly done by generating a large dataset of teacher outputs (completions, reasoning traces, or even soft probability distributions over tokens) for a wide range of prompts, then fine-tuning the smaller student on that dataset.

Why this matters

A large frontier model is expensive and slow to run at scale, but it 'knows' patterns that are hard to get a small model to learn from raw internet text alone. Distillation transfers a meaningful fraction of the teacher's behavior into a model that's far cheaper and faster to serve, which is exactly the trade-off production systems care about: most requests don't need frontier-level capability, they need 'good enough, fast, and cheap', and a distilled model can hit that bar for a specific narrowed task distribution even though it will never match the teacher's general capability.

How it works

Classic distillation (used originally for smaller classifiers) trains the student to match the teacher's full output probability distribution (soft labels), not just the single top answer, because the relative probabilities across wrong answers still carry useful signal about how confident or uncertain the teacher was. For LLMs, a common practical approach is response distillation: sample many high-quality completions (including chain-of-thought reasoning) from the teacher across a representative prompt set, then supervised-fine-tune the smaller student model on those teacher-generated examples, effectively transferring the teacher's demonstrated behavior rather than its exact probability distribution, since providers rarely expose full logits for closed models.

When to use it

you have a narrow, well-defined task distribution where a large model performs well, and you want a much cheaper/faster model for high-volume production traffic on that same distribution, and you can generate or already have a large set of representative teacher outputs.

When not to use it

the target task needs broad, open-ended general capability the small student can't realistically absorb from a feasible amount of distillation data, or the task distribution in production will drift significantly from what the distillation dataset covered, causing the student to underperform outside its narrow training distribution.
keyPoints: Distillation trains a smaller student model to mimic a larger teacher's outputs, transferring behavior rather than training the student from raw data alone.
The core motivation is cost/latency at scale: most production traffic doesn't need frontier-level general capability for a narrow task.

For LLMs, response distillation (fine-tuning on sampled teacher completions, including reasoning traces) is more common than classic soft-label logit matching, since closed models rarely expose full logits.
Best fit: narrow, well-defined task distribution with representative teacher outputs available and high-volume production traffic.
Avoid when: the task needs broad general capability, or production traffic will drift outside the distillation dataset's coverage.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Your product uses a frontier model for a high-volume classification-and-tagging feature, and the inference bill is now a major cost line. Leadership asks if you can 'just use a smaller model'. How do you approach this?
blocks.answer:
I would frame this as a distillation candidate specifically because the task is narrow (classification and tagging) and high-volume, which is exactly the profile where a small, cheap model can match a frontier model's accuracy on the specific task even though it can't match its general capability.

First I would build an eval set from real production inputs with the frontier model's outputs treated as a reasonable proxy for ground truth (validated by a smaller human-labeled sample), then use the frontier model to generate a larger training set of labeled examples across the actual distribution of inputs seen in production, being careful to include edge cases and the minority classes that are usually underrepresented.

I would fine-tune a much smaller open or lower-tier model on that generated dataset, then evaluate the student against the same eval set the frontier model was scored on, measuring both agreement rate with the frontier model and, more importantly, agreement with the validated human labels, since a student that just learns to mimic the teacher's mistakes isn't actually a win.

If the student's accuracy on the held-out eval is acceptably close to the frontier model's, I would roll it out behind a routing layer that sends only the classification/tagging traffic to the cheap model and keeps the frontier model as a fallback for low-confidence or out-of-distribution cases, then monitor accuracy on live traffic over time since real-world input distribution will drift from the training snapshot.
hints: Recognize narrow, high-volume tasks as a strong distillation fit versus general capability tasks.
Generate a representative training set from the teacher and validate against real human labels, not just teacher agreement.
Roll out with a routing/fallback strategy and monitor for distribution drift over time.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.code:
def build_distillation_dataset(prompts, teacher_call):
    examples = []
    for prompt in prompts:
        teacher_output = teacher_call(prompt)  # sample from the large teacher model
        examples.append({"prompt": prompt, "completion": teacher_output})
    return examples

# examples is then used as a standard supervised fine-tuning dataset
# for the smaller student model.
blocks.explanation: Practical LLM distillation is usually just supervised fine-tuning where the labels are generated by sampling the teacher model rather than hand-labeled by humans, which is what makes it scalable to large datasets.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Assuming distillation will produce a smaller model with 'basically the same' general capability as the teacher, without acknowledging it only transfers behavior for the specific distribution covered by the distillation dataset.
blocks.whyItHappens: Marketing around smaller distilled models often emphasizes benchmark scores close to the teacher, which can be true on the specific benchmark distribution used, while masking that performance gaps reappear on inputs further from that training distribution.
blocks.correctApproach: Be explicit that distillation transfers task-specific behavior proportional to how representative the training data is; validate the student against an independent, held-out eval set covering the real production distribution, not just agreement with the teacher on the training-adjacent data.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: Distillation trades a bounded amount of accuracy on the narrow task for a large reduction in inference cost and latency; the trade only pays off if the task distribution is stable and well covered by the distillation dataset.
keyPoints: Validate the student against real human-labeled ground truth, not just agreement with the teacher.
Include edge cases and minority classes in the distillation dataset; they're usually underrepresented and disproportionately affect accuracy.
Monitor live accuracy after rollout and keep a fallback to the teacher model for low-confidence or out-of-distribution cases.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: Why might a distilled student sometimes outperform the teacher on a narrow task?
blocks.answer: A student fine-tuned specifically on that narrow task distribution can become more specialized and less distracted by unrelated general capability than the teacher, especially if the teacher's outputs were filtered or curated to remove low-quality examples before distillation, effectively giving the student a cleaner, more focused training signal for that specific task.

title: Choosing a Model for a Task
description: Model choice is a trade-off between capability, latency, cost and data sensitivity, and the right answer is often a smaller model plus good context rather than the largest model available.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

Picking a model is not 'pick the smartest one'; it's balancing four axes at once: raw capability (can it actually do this reasoning/generation task well), latency (how fast does a response need to come back), cost per request at your expected volume, and data sensitivity (can this data leave your infrastructure to a third-party API at all). The largest, most capable model wins on the first axis and usually loses on the other three.

Why this matters

Many teams default to the flagship model for everything, which quietly multiplies cost and latency across every request without checking whether the task actually needed that capability. A classification, extraction or short-answer task often performs just as well on a much smaller/cheaper model, especially once you've invested in good prompting or a bit of fine-tuning, while a genuinely hard multi-step reasoning or code-generation task may need the frontier model regardless of cost. Getting this wrong either wastes money at scale or under-delivers quality on the tasks that actually need it.

How it works

In practice this becomes a routing decision: classify incoming requests by required capability (simple lookup/format tasks vs. complex reasoning) and send each to the cheapest model tier that reliably handles it, often validated empirically rather than by intuition, since a smaller model plus a well-engineered prompt and retrieved context frequently matches a larger model's accuracy on narrower tasks at a fraction of the cost. Data sensitivity constrains this further: some data cannot leave your VPC or country, or contractually cannot go to certain vendors, which can eliminate an otherwise-good model choice entirely regardless of its capability or price, pushing you toward self-hosted open-weight models.

When to use it

building any system with meaningful request volume, where cost or latency at scale matters, or where any part of the data has compliance/sensitivity constraints that must be checked before a vendor is chosen.

When not to use it

very low-volume, exploratory or prototype work where iteration speed matters far more than cost, and just using the strongest available model to validate the idea first is the right call before optimizing model choice.
keyPoints: Model choice balances capability, latency, cost and data sensitivity, not just raw capability.
The flagship model is frequently overkill for narrow tasks; a smaller model with good prompting/context often matches it at a fraction of the cost.
Data sensitivity and compliance constraints can eliminate an otherwise-ideal model choice regardless of capability or price.
Best fit: any system with real request volume, where routing to the cheapest sufficient model tier matters.
Avoid when: early prototyping, where using the strongest model to validate the idea beats optimizing cost prematurely.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Your app currently sends every request, from simple FAQ lookups to complex multi-step analysis, to the same flagship model, and your CFO just flagged the inference bill. How do you redesign the model strategy?
blocks.answer:
I would start by profiling actual production traffic to see the real distribution of task difficulty, because I'd bet a large share of requests are simple lookups, classification or short-answer tasks that don't need flagship-level reasoning at all. Treating every request as equally hard is the root cause of the cost problem, not the model choice itself.

I'd build a lightweight router, which could itself be a small, cheap model or even a simpler heuristic/classifier, that tags each incoming request by required capability, then sends simple requests to a smaller, cheaper model and reserves the flagship model for requests that genuinely need multi-step reasoning, long context synthesis, or high-stakes accuracy.

Before trusting this in production, I would build an eval set spanning both easy and hard requests and measure the smaller model's accuracy against the flagship model's on the easy bucket specifically, since the whole strategy depends on the smaller model actually being good enough there, not just cheaper. I'd also add a fallback: if the small model's response is flagged low-confidence or fails a quick validation check, escalate that specific request to the flagship model rather than accepting a wrong answer to save money.

Finally I'd track cost-per-resolved-request and quality metrics per tier after rollout, since the goal isn't just lowering the bill, it's making sure quality on the hard requests, which is what the CFO's cost-cutting shouldn't be allowed to quietly degrade, stays intact.
hints: Profile actual traffic difficulty distribution before assuming every request needs the flagship model.
Build a router that sends easy requests to a cheaper model and reserves the flagship model for hard ones.
Validate the smaller model's accuracy against an eval set and add an escalation fallback for low-confidence cases.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.explanation: A cheap upfront classification step routes the majority of simple requests to a low-cost model, reserving the expensive flagship model only for the smaller share of requests that actually need it, which is where most of the cost savings comes from at scale.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Defaulting to 'just use the best/largest model available' for every part of a system, treating model choice as a one-time decision rather than a per-task trade-off.
blocks.whyItHappens: The largest model is the safest-feeling choice during early development because it minimizes the chance of a capability-related failure, and teams often don't revisit that default once it's in production and traffic (and cost) scales up.
blocks.correctApproach: Profile the actual task distribution, measure whether a smaller/cheaper model meets the bar on an eval set for each task category, and route by required capability rather than using one model tier for everything.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: The most expensive model is a ceiling on capability, not a default; the right model per task is whichever cheapest option clears your accuracy bar on real eval data, with data sensitivity constraints checked before any vendor is chosen.
keyPoints: Build task-specific eval sets before deciding a smaller model is 'good enough' for that task.
Check data residency and compliance constraints early; they can eliminate model options regardless of capability or cost.
Revisit model choice periodically as traffic mix and provider pricing/capability change, not just once at launch.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: How would you decide between a hosted API model and a self-hosted open-weight model?
blocks.answer: It comes down to data sensitivity, volume economics and operational capacity: a hosted API is simpler and often cheaper at low-to-moderate volume with no infra burden, while self-hosting an open-weight model becomes attractive at high sustained volume, when data cannot leave your infrastructure, or when you need deep customization the API doesn't expose, in exchange for taking on GPU infrastructure and serving complexity yourself.

title: Evaluating LLM Outputs
description: Evaluating an LLM feature means defining task-specific success criteria upfront, because generic fluency says nothing about whether the answer was actually correct or useful.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

An LLM will almost always produce fluent, well-formatted, confident-sounding text, whether it's right or wrong, which means 'does it sound good' is useless as a quality signal. Evaluation means defining, before you ship, what a correct or acceptable output actually looks like for your specific task, then measuring outputs against that definition, not against general impressions.

Why this matters

Without task-specific criteria, teams ship on vibes: a few example outputs look good in a demo, then the feature breaks in ways nobody predicted because nothing was actually measured against a rubric. Different tasks need fundamentally different metrics: an extraction task can be scored with exact-match or F1 against structured ground truth, a summarization task needs criteria like faithfulness and coverage, an open-ended chat task might need human or LLM-judge ratings against a rubric, and each of these needs a different evaluation setup entirely.

How it works

Start from the failure modes that actually matter for the product, not generic quality. Build a representative eval set of real or realistic inputs, ideally including known-hard and edge cases, not just easy average-case examples. Define per-task metrics: for tasks with a verifiable ground truth, use exact/structural comparison; for open-ended generation, use a rubric scored by humans or a calibrated LLM judge, and for factual tasks, explicitly check groundedness against the source rather than just fluency. Track these metrics over time so you can tell whether a prompt, model or pipeline change is actually an improvement rather than trusting a handful of manually reviewed examples.

When to use it

any LLM feature before it ships, and continuously after, since prompts, models and data all drift and a passing eval today doesn't guarantee correctness after the next change.

When not to use it

pure throwaway prototyping where you're validating a rough idea manually before investing in a formal eval set is reasonable, but this should be a short phase, not a permanent substitute for measurement once the feature is real.
keyPoints: Fluent output is not correct output; evaluation requires task-specific success criteria defined before you measure.
Different tasks need different metrics: exact-match/F1 for extraction, faithfulness/coverage for summarization, rubric-based judging for open-ended generation.
Build a representative eval set including known-hard and edge cases, not just easy average-case examples.
Best fit: any LLM feature before shipping and continuously afterward, since drift is constant.
Avoid when: pure early prototyping, where manual review is acceptable for a short phase before real measurement is needed.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: A stakeholder says 'the new prompt looks great, I tried five examples and they all looked right, let's ship it.' How do you respond as the engineer responsible for this feature's quality?
blocks.answer:
I would acknowledge that five good examples are a useful sanity check but not evidence of production readiness, because five hand-picked examples almost never include the edge cases and hard inputs that actually cause failures at scale, and 'looked right' is a subjective, unmeasured judgment that won't catch subtle correctness issues like a slightly wrong number or an unsupported claim.

I would propose we run this against our existing eval set, or build one if it doesn't exist yet, covering the range of real inputs this feature will see, including known-hard cases like ambiguous phrasing, edge-case data, and adversarial inputs, and score it against explicit criteria for this task, not general impressions.

I would specifically compare the new prompt's eval score against the current production prompt's score on the same eval set, since 'better in five examples' doesn't tell us whether it's better or worse on the full distribution, and a change that improves five examples can regress accuracy elsewhere if it wasn't tested broadly.

If building a full eval set isn't feasible before this specific ship date, I'd propose a scoped compromise: ship behind a flag to a small percentage of traffic with monitoring on the specific failure signals we care about, rather than a full rollout based on five manually reviewed examples, so we get real signal before broad exposure.
hints: Explain why a handful of hand-picked examples doesn't represent the real input distribution.
Propose comparing against the current production prompt on the same eval set, not in isolation.
Offer a scoped, monitored rollout as a fallback if a full eval set isn't ready in time.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.code:
def run_eval(eval_set, generate_fn, score_fn):
    results = []
    for case in eval_set:
        output = generate_fn(case["input"])
        score = score_fn(output, case["expected"])
        results.append({"id": case["id"], "score": score, "output": output})
    avg_score = sum(r["score"] for r in results) / len(results)
    return avg_score, results

# score_fn is task-specific: exact match, F1, groundedness check, or LLM-judge rubric.
blocks.explanation: The eval harness itself is generic; what makes it meaningful is the task-specific score_fn and a representative eval_set that actually reflects the inputs and failure modes the feature will encounter in production.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Judging LLM output quality by reading a handful of examples and forming a subjective impression, without a defined rubric, ground truth, or representative eval set.
blocks.whyItHappens: LLM outputs are readable natural language, which makes it deceptively easy to feel confident about quality just by eyeballing a few responses, unlike a numeric model output that obviously needs a defined metric before anyone would trust it.
blocks.correctApproach: Define task-specific success criteria and build a representative eval set before judging quality, then measure changes against that fixed baseline rather than re-forming an impression from a new handful of examples each time.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: Building and maintaining a good eval set has a real upfront cost, but it's the only way to detect regressions from prompt, model or pipeline changes before users do; skipping it trades a small time investment now for unpredictable production failures later.
keyPoints: Include known-hard and edge cases in the eval set, not just easy average-case examples.
Pick a metric that matches the task's actual failure mode, not a generic fluency or length score.
Compare every change against the current production baseline on the same eval set, not in isolation.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: How large does an eval set need to be to trust its results?
blocks.answer: It depends on the variance of your scoring metric and how large a quality difference you need to detect; a rough rule of thumb is dozens to a few hundred representative, diverse cases for early signal, but for detecting small regressions reliably you typically need enough cases that the score difference between two versions is larger than the noise from case-to-case variance, which you can check with a simple significance or confidence-interval calculation rather than guessing.

title: LLM-as-Judge
description: Using one model to grade another model's outputs against a rubric scales evaluation cheaply, but the judge itself needs calibration against human ratings to be trusted.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

Instead of paying humans to rate every output for open-ended tasks (summarization quality, helpfulness, tone), you prompt a capable LLM with the input, the output, and a scoring rubric, and have it return a score or a pairwise preference ('response A vs response B'). This scales evaluation to thousands of examples at a fraction of the cost and turnaround time of human review.

Why this matters

Human evaluation is the gold standard for open-ended quality but is slow and expensive, which makes it impractical to run on every prompt or model change. LLM-as-judge fills that gap, but it inherits real biases: judges tend to prefer longer responses (verbosity bias), prefer the first option shown in a pairwise comparison (position bias), and can be fooled by confident, well-formatted but subtly wrong content, the same reward-hacking-adjacent failure modes that show up in RLHF reward models. An uncalibrated judge can therefore systematically rank actually-worse outputs higher.

How it works

You write a rubric-based judge prompt with clear scoring criteria and, ideally, few-shot examples of what different score levels look like, then run it over your eval set. For pairwise comparisons, you randomize which response is shown first (A/B) and run it both ways to detect and cancel out position bias. Critically, you calibrate the judge by running it against a smaller set of examples that also have human ratings, checking agreement rate between judge and human, and iterating on the rubric or few-shot examples until agreement is high enough to trust the judge on the larger uncalibrated set. Some teams use a stronger/different model as judge than the model being evaluated, to reduce the risk of a model being biased toward its own output style.

When to use it

you need to evaluate open-ended quality (helpfulness, coherence, adherence to a style) at a scale where human review isn't feasible, and you've calibrated the judge against a human-rated sample first.

When not to use it

the task has objective, checkable ground truth (exact answer, structured extraction), where a direct comparison is more reliable and cheaper than an LLM judge; or you haven't calibrated the judge at all, in which case its scores are unverified and can mislead decisions.
keyPoints: LLM-as-judge scores or compares outputs against a rubric, scaling evaluation far beyond what human review can cover.
Known judge biases include verbosity bias, position bias in pairwise comparisons, and being fooled by confident but wrong content.
Calibrate the judge against a human-rated sample and randomize A/B order before trusting it at scale.
Best fit: open-ended quality evaluation at scale, after calibration against human ratings.
Avoid when: the task has objective checkable ground truth, or the judge hasn't been calibrated at all.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: You set up an LLM judge to A/B test two prompt versions for a summarization feature, and it reports Prompt B wins 80% of the time. Before you ship Prompt B, what do you check?
blocks.answer:
I would first check for position bias by re-running the same comparisons with A and B swapped in the judge prompt; if the win rate flips or shrinks substantially when the order is reversed, the 80% figure was largely an artifact of which response the judge saw first, not a real quality difference.

Next I would check for verbosity or formatting bias: if Prompt B's outputs are simply longer or more heavily formatted with bullet points and headers, the judge may be rewarding surface features rather than actual summary quality like faithfulness and coverage of the source. I'd control for this by including length and format-neutral rubric criteria explicitly in the judge prompt, or by testing whether the win rate holds when outputs are length-normalized.

Then I would validate the judge itself against a smaller human-rated sample of the same comparisons: pull maybe 30-50 of the disputed cases, get human ratings, and check the judge's agreement rate with humans specifically on this task. If agreement is low, the 80% figure isn't trustworthy regardless of how confident the judge sounds.

Only after position bias is ruled out, surface-feature bias is controlled for, and the judge's agreement with human raters is validated on a sample, would I trust the 80% win rate enough to ship Prompt B, and even then I'd keep monitoring real user feedback signals after rollout as a final check.
hints: Check for position bias by swapping A/B order and seeing if the result holds.
Control for verbosity/formatting bias that can fool the judge independent of actual quality.
Validate judge agreement against a human-rated sample before trusting the win rate.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.explanation: Explicit rubric dimensions (faithfulness, coverage) reduce the judge's reliance on surface features like length, and running the comparison in both orders lets you detect and discount position bias before trusting the result.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Treating an LLM judge's score as ground truth without calibrating it against human ratings or checking for known biases like verbosity and position bias.
blocks.whyItHappens: An LLM judge returns a clean numeric score that looks objective, which creates false confidence that it's measuring the real thing, when in fact it's a model with its own learned preferences that can systematically diverge from what humans actually value.
blocks.correctApproach: Calibrate the judge against a human-rated sample, measure agreement rate, and explicitly test for and control known biases (position, verbosity, formatting) before treating the judge's scores as a reliable signal for shipping decisions.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: LLM-as-judge trades some accuracy and introduces its own biases in exchange for massive scale and speed over human evaluation; it's a good complement to, not a full replacement for, periodic human review, especially for high-stakes decisions.
keyPoints: Randomize and swap A/B order in every pairwise comparison to detect position bias.
Use explicit rubric dimensions rather than a single holistic score to reduce surface-feature bias.
Periodically re-validate judge agreement with humans, since drift in either the judge model or the task can silently erode calibration.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: Should the judge model be the same model you're evaluating?
blocks.answer: Generally no, or at least not exclusively; using the same model as both generator and judge risks self-preference bias where the model rates outputs in its own style more favorably, so it's safer to use a different or stronger model as judge, or validate with a human-rated sample regardless of which model judges.

title: Hallucination Detection
description: A hallucination is a fluent, confident statement that is not supported by the model's training data or provided context, and catching it requires checking claims against a source, not just checking that the text sounds right.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

A hallucination is content the model states with normal confident fluency that is not actually grounded in anything true, whether that's an invented citation, a wrong API parameter, or a fabricated fact contradicting the provided context. The model has no internal 'I don't know' signal in the way a database does; it generates the statistically likely next tokens regardless of whether they're true, so a confident tone is not evidence of correctness.

Why this matters

Hallucinations are the single most cited production risk for LLM features because they look identical to correct answers on the surface, fluent, specific, well-formatted, which makes them dangerous exactly where users are most likely to trust the output without checking it, like a legal summary or a code suggestion with a nonexistent library function. Catching them requires an explicit verification step against a ground truth source, not better prompting alone, since prompting can reduce but not eliminate the underlying cause.

How it works

Detection approaches fall into a few families: groundedness checking, verifying each factual claim in the output is actually supported by the retrieved context or source document (often done with a second LLM call or a natural language inference model that checks entailment between claim and source); self-consistency checking, sampling the model multiple times at nonzero temperature and flagging claims that vary across samples as less reliable, since consistently repeated claims are more likely grounded than one-off ones; and external verification, checking specific claim types (citations, API signatures, numeric facts) against an authoritative source via a tool call rather than trusting the model's assertion. RAG reduces hallucination risk by giving the model real context to ground in, but doesn't eliminate it, since the model can still ignore or misread the provided context and hallucinate anyway.

When to use it

any feature where a wrong but confident-sounding claim has real cost (legal, medical, financial, code generation, citations), which should get an explicit groundedness or verification check before the output reaches a user.

When not to use it

low-stakes creative or brainstorming tasks where 'factual grounding' isn't actually the point of the output, and adding verification overhead doesn't serve the task.
keyPoints: A hallucination is a confidently stated but ungrounded claim; fluent tone is never evidence of correctness.
Detection families: groundedness/entailment checking against source, self-consistency across samples, and external verification via tools for specific claim types.
RAG reduces but does not eliminate hallucination risk, since the model can still ignore or misread provided context.
Best fit: any feature where a wrong confident claim has real cost, needing an explicit verification step before output reaches a user.
Avoid when: low-stakes creative/brainstorming tasks where factual grounding isn't the point.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Your RAG-based support assistant confidently cited a refund policy detail that doesn't exist anywhere in your actual documentation, and a user acted on it. How do you both root-cause this and prevent recurrence?
blocks.answer:
I would first check whether this was a retrieval failure or a generation failure, since they need different fixes. I'd look at what chunks were actually retrieved and passed to the model for that query; if the correct policy chunk was never retrieved, the model effectively had no grounding for that specific detail and filled the gap from its general training-data priors, which is a retrieval problem, fixable by improving chunking, embeddings, or query reformulation.

If the correct chunk was retrieved but the model still stated something not actually in it, that's a generation-side hallucination where the model ignored or misread the provided context, and the fix is adding an explicit groundedness check: after generating the answer, run a second pass (either a separate model call or an entailment check) that verifies each factual claim in the answer is actually supported by the retrieved chunks, and block or flag any claim that isn't.

For this specific class of high-stakes claim (refund policy, money-related), I would go further and require the answer to include an inline citation back to the specific retrieved passage, and reject any generated answer that makes a policy claim without a matching citation, rather than relying on the model to self-police its own groundedness.

Finally, I'd add this exact query to my eval set as a regression case, audit for other high-stakes claim types (policy, pricing, legal) that deserve the same mandatory-citation treatment, and consider a lower-confidence fallback response ('let me connect you with a human for policy questions') for any claim that fails the groundedness check rather than showing a possibly-wrong answer.
hints: Distinguish a retrieval failure (chunk never retrieved) from a generation failure (context ignored).
Add an explicit groundedness/entailment check as a second pass, not just better prompting.
For high-stakes claim types, require mandatory citations and a safe fallback when grounding fails.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.explanation: This is a minimal entailment-style groundedness check: each factual claim extracted from the answer is checked against the retrieved context independently, and any claim not supported by the context is flagged before the answer is shown to a user.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Saying 'we added RAG so hallucinations are handled' as if retrieval alone eliminates the problem, without an explicit check that the generated answer actually used the retrieved context correctly.
blocks.whyItHappens: RAG measurably reduces hallucination rate in most systems, which leads to the false generalization that it solves the problem entirely, when in reality the model can still generate claims not supported by, or contradicting, the exact context it was given.
blocks.correctApproach: Treat RAG as risk reduction, not elimination, and add an explicit groundedness/citation check on the generated answer against the retrieved context, especially for high-stakes claim types, rather than assuming retrieval alone guarantees faithfulness.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: Every hallucination-detection method adds latency and cost (a second model call, multiple samples, or a tool lookup), so apply the strongest checks to the highest-stakes claim types and accept lighter or no verification for low-stakes generative tasks.
keyPoints: Distinguish retrieval failures from generation failures when a hallucination is reported; they need different fixes.
Require inline citations and reject ungrounded claims for high-stakes categories like policy, pricing, legal or medical content.
Track hallucination rate as an explicit eval metric over time, not just as anecdotal user reports.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: Can self-consistency (sampling multiple times) alone catch hallucinations?
blocks.answer: It catches some, since claims the model states inconsistently across samples are more likely fabricated, but it misses hallucinations the model states confidently and consistently every time, so it should be combined with, not substituted for, groundedness checking against an actual source.

title: Golden Datasets and Regression Testing
description: A golden dataset is a curated, versioned set of inputs with known-good outputs that lets you detect when a prompt, model or pipeline change silently breaks something that used to work.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

A golden dataset is the LLM-system equivalent of a unit test suite: a fixed, version-controlled collection of representative inputs paired with known-correct or known-acceptable outputs (or scoring criteria), that you re-run after any change to the prompt, model version, or retrieval pipeline to check nothing that used to work has quietly broken.

Why this matters

LLM systems don't fail loudly like a compiler error; a prompt tweak meant to fix one issue can silently degrade accuracy on a different case, and a model provider's silent version update behind an API alias can shift behavior across your whole system at once. Without a fixed dataset to re-run, these regressions are invisible until users notice, often far downstream of the change that caused them.

How it works

Curate cases from real production traffic (anonymized/scrubbed of sensitive data as needed), covering common cases, known historical failure cases (bugs you already fixed once), and edge cases, then freeze the set with version control alongside your code so it evolves deliberately, not accidentally. Every case gets an expected output, an acceptance range, or a scoring rubric depending on the task. Run the full set automatically whenever the prompt, model, or pipeline changes, ideally as part of CI, and compare aggregate and per-case scores against the last known-good baseline; a specific case that used to pass and now fails is exactly the regression signal you want surfaced before shipping.

When to use it

any LLM feature that has shipped and will be iterated on, since the entire value is catching regressions across changes over time, including changes you don't control like a provider updating a model behind a pinned alias.

When not to use it

during the very earliest exploratory phase before the feature's behavior and success criteria have stabilized enough to define 'known-good' outputs meaningfully; building the golden set too early can lock in premature assumptions about correct behavior.
keyPoints: A golden dataset is a version-controlled regression suite: fixed inputs with known-good outputs, re-run after every prompt/model/pipeline change.
LLM regressions are silent by default; a golden set is what turns them into a visible, comparable signal.
Include known historical failure cases (already-fixed bugs) so regressions of past fixes get caught automatically.
Best fit: any shipped LLM feature under ongoing iteration, including exposure to silent provider-side model updates.
Avoid when: very early exploratory phase before success criteria have stabilized enough to define known-good outputs.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Three weeks after you fixed a bug where the assistant gave wrong shipping-cost answers, a very similar bug resurfaces after an unrelated prompt change for a different feature. How do you make sure this class of regression can't sneak back in silently again?
blocks.answer:
I would first check whether the original shipping-cost bug fix was ever added as a permanent case in a golden/regression dataset; if it wasn't, that's the root process gap, since manual verification at fix-time doesn't protect against a later unrelated change reintroducing the same failure.

I would add the exact failing case (the input that triggered the original bug and the correct expected output) to the golden dataset now, along with a few close variations, so the specific failure mode, not just that one exact input, gets covered going forward.

I'd wire the golden dataset to run automatically whenever the prompt or pipeline changes, as part of the same review process as a code change, so a regression on this case is caught before merge, not three weeks after a different, seemingly unrelated change ships.

I would also look at why an unrelated prompt change affected this behavior at all, since that often points to prompt sections that aren't actually independent (a shared system prompt or shared instruction block), and I'd consider restructuring the prompt so unrelated feature instructions are less likely to interact, in addition to relying on the regression test as a safety net.
hints: Check whether the original bug fix was ever captured as a permanent regression case.
Add the case and variations to the golden dataset and automate it in the change/review process.
Investigate why an unrelated change affected this behavior, since shared prompt structure is a common cause.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.code:
{
  "id": "shipping-cost-international-regression",
  "input": "How much is shipping to Canada for a 2kg package?",
  "expected_contains": ["international shipping rate", "customs"],
  "expected_excludes": ["free shipping"],
  "source": "bug-1042, fixed 2026-07-01",
  "category": "regression"
}
blocks.explanation: Each golden case is versioned with a traceable source (which bug or requirement it came from), plus explicit pass/fail criteria that can be checked automatically, turning what used to be a manual re-verification into a repeatable, auditable test.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Manually re-checking a handful of examples after each prompt change instead of maintaining a fixed, version-controlled dataset that gets run automatically and compared against a baseline.
blocks.whyItHappens: Manual spot-checking feels sufficient because each individual change seems small, but it doesn't scale: nobody remembers to re-check every past bug fix against every new change, so old failure modes silently resurface once memory of the original bug fades.
blocks.correctApproach: Maintain a growing, version-controlled golden dataset that includes past bug fixes as permanent regression cases, and run it automatically on every prompt, model or pipeline change, comparing against the last known-good baseline rather than relying on memory.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: Maintaining a golden dataset has an ongoing curation cost, since it needs to grow with real failure modes and stay representative as the product changes, but the alternative, discovering regressions from user complaints, is far more expensive in trust and cleanup.
keyPoints: Add every fixed bug's triggering case to the golden dataset as a permanent regression test.
Run the golden dataset automatically as part of the change process, not as an optional manual step.
Periodically prune or refresh cases that no longer reflect real production traffic, so the set doesn't drift into testing irrelevant scenarios.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: How do you handle a golden dataset case when the model provider silently updates the underlying model behind a pinned API alias?
blocks.answer: Run the full golden dataset against the new model behavior as soon as it's detected (via monitoring or provider changelogs), treat any newly failing case as a real regression regardless of whose change caused it, and where possible pin to an explicit dated model version rather than a rolling alias to control exactly when such changes take effect.

title: Benchmarks and Their Limits
description: Public benchmarks are useful for comparing raw model capability, but they rarely resemble your actual task closely enough to substitute for evaluation on your own data.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

Public benchmarks (MMLU, HumanEval, GSM8K, and many others) score models on fixed, standardized test sets designed to measure broad capability along a specific axis, like general knowledge, code generation, or math reasoning. They're useful for comparing models against each other on that axis, but a benchmark score tells you almost nothing about how that model will perform on your specific task with your specific data and prompt.

Why this matters

Benchmarks are static and public, which creates two real problems: contamination, where benchmark questions or near-duplicates leak into a model's training data, inflating scores without reflecting genuine generalization, and distribution mismatch, where your actual production inputs, domain-specific terminology, unusual formatting, adversarial users, look nothing like a benchmark's clean, well-formed question set. A model that tops a leaderboard can still underperform a lower-ranked model on your narrow task, especially after prompting or fine-tuning are factored in.

How it works

Use benchmarks for what they're good for: a first-pass filter to narrow down candidate models before investing in your own evaluation, and a way to track whether a new model generation improved on a capability axis relevant to your use case. Then always run your own task-specific eval set, built from your real data and failure modes, before making a final model decision, since that's the only measurement that reflects your actual deployment. Watch for benchmark-specific quirks too, like a model being specifically fine-tuned to perform well on a popular benchmark's format without a corresponding gain in general capability.

When to use it

early-stage model shortlisting, tracking broad capability trends across model generations, or when no domain-specific eval data exists yet and a rough capability signal is better than nothing.

When not to use it

as the sole basis for a final model choice or for claiming a specific feature will work well, since a benchmark's distribution is very unlikely to match your production traffic closely enough for that.
keyPoints: Benchmarks measure broad capability on a fixed axis; they don't measure how a model performs on your specific task and data.
Contamination (benchmark data leaking into training) and distribution mismatch (clean test questions vs messy real traffic) both limit how much a benchmark score generalizes.
Use benchmarks to shortlist candidate models, never as the final basis for a production decision.
Best fit: early model shortlisting or tracking capability trends across model generations.
Avoid when: making a final model decision or claiming production performance without your own task-specific eval.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: A vendor pitches their model by pointing to a top score on a well-known coding benchmark, proposing you switch your code-review assistant to it. How do you evaluate this claim?
blocks.answer:
I would treat the benchmark score as a reason to shortlist the model for testing, not as evidence it will perform well on our actual task, since a coding benchmark like HumanEval mostly tests generating short, self-contained functions from a clear spec, which is quite different from reviewing real, messy, multi-file production code with implicit context and team-specific conventions.

I would ask the vendor, or check independently, whether there's public discussion of contamination concerns for that benchmark and that model family, since a high score partly explained by benchmark-adjacent training data wouldn't predict real-world generalization.

Then I would run our own eval set: a curated collection of real past code review comments from our repositories, with the expected type of feedback (bug found, style issue, missed edge case) as ground truth, and measure the candidate model against our current model on that same set, scoring for precision (how often flagged issues are real) and recall (how often real issues are caught), since those are what actually matter for a review assistant.

Only if the candidate model performs better on our own eval set, and ideally after a limited real-world trial on a subset of actual PRs with human review of its comments, would I recommend switching, regardless of how strong the vendor's benchmark story is.
hints: Note the mismatch between what the benchmark tests and what code review actually requires.
Consider contamination risk when a vendor leads with a top benchmark score.
Insist on your own task-specific eval set and a limited real trial before switching.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.explanation: The decision-relevant comparison is always the candidate model versus your current model on your own eval set; public benchmark scores may justify including a model in this comparison but shouldn't substitute for running it.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Choosing or justifying a model switch primarily by citing a public leaderboard rank, without running any task-specific evaluation on real data.
blocks.whyItHappens: Benchmark leaderboards are the most visible, easily comparable signal available, and citing a number feels more rigorous than 'we tried it and it felt better', even though the number often doesn't transfer to the specific task at hand.
blocks.correctApproach: Use benchmark rank only to shortlist candidates, then always validate with your own task-specific eval set built from real data and failure modes before making a final decision.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: Benchmarks are cheap and fast to check but low-fidelity for your specific task; your own eval set is expensive to build and maintain but is the only reliable signal for a production decision, so use each for what it's good at.
keyPoints: Treat benchmark scores as a shortlist filter, not a final decision criterion.
Watch for contamination and benchmark-specific overfitting when a score seems unusually high.
Always validate a model swap against your own eval set and, ideally, a limited real-traffic trial.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: Why can a model that scores lower on a general benchmark still be the better choice for your product?
blocks.answer: Because your task's success criteria and input distribution likely differ substantially from the benchmark's, and a model that's cheaper, faster, or specifically strong on the narrow skill your product needs can outperform a broadly stronger model on your actual task once you measure with your own eval set.
