title: Model Routing and Fallback
description: Model routing sends each request to the cheapest model that can handle it and falls back to a stronger model or a cached/default response when a call fails or a provider is down.

blocks.title: Simple but deep explanation
blocks.content:
Simple explanation

Model routing is a request-time decision layer that picks which model handles a given request based on its estimated difficulty, cost budget, or latency requirement, rather than sending every request to one fixed model. Fallback is a related but distinct concern: what happens when the chosen model call fails outright (timeout, error, provider outage, rate limit), which needs a defined recovery path so a single provider incident doesn't take down your whole feature.

Why this matters

Without routing, you either overpay by sending simple requests to an expensive model, or underperform by sending hard requests to a cheap model that can't handle them; without fallback, a transient provider issue (rate limiting, an outage, a timeout) becomes a full outage for your feature even though the failure was temporary and external. Both are core production-reliability and cost-control concerns that are easy to skip in early development when you're calling one model directly and everything just works.

How it works

Routing is typically implemented with a lightweight upfront classification step (a cheap model, embedding-based similarity to known request types, or simple heuristics like prompt length or presence of certain keywords) that estimates request difficulty or category, then dispatches to the model tier best matched to that estimate, with a way to escalate mid-request if the cheap model's response looks low-confidence or fails a validation check. Fallback typically follows a defined chain: retry the same model with backoff for transient errors, fall back to a different provider or model tier if retries are exhausted or the provider is confirmed down, and as a last resort return a cached/default response or a graceful degraded message rather than a raw error, always logging which path was taken so reliability issues are visible in monitoring rather than silently absorbed.

When to use it

routing: any production system with a real mix of request difficulty and meaningful request volume, where the cost/quality trade-off is worth actively managing. Fallback: any production system depending on a third-party model API, since provider outages, rate limits and transient errors are a matter of when, not if, at sufficient scale and time.

When not to use it

routing: a system with a narrow, uniform task distribution where one model tier is clearly correct for everything, making a routing layer unnecessary complexity. Fallback: extremely low-stakes internal tools where an occasional failed request with a simple error message is genuinely acceptable and doesn't warrant the added complexity of a fallback chain.
keyPoints: Routing picks the model per request based on estimated difficulty/cost/latency needs; fallback defines recovery when a model call fails outright.
Without routing you overpay on easy requests or underperform on hard ones; without fallback a transient provider issue becomes a full feature outage.
Routing uses a lightweight upfront classifier or heuristic; fallback follows a defined chain (retry with backoff, then alternate provider/model, then cached/default response).
Best fit for routing: real mix of request difficulty at meaningful volume; best fit for fallback: any dependency on a third-party model API.
Avoid when: routing adds unneeded complexity for a uniform task distribution, or fallback overhead isn't justified for very low-stakes internal tools.

blocks.title: Scenario question
blocks.question: Your primary model provider had a 40-minute outage last week and your entire AI feature returned errors to every user for that whole window. Leadership wants this to never happen again. How do you design for it?
blocks.answer:
I would design an explicit fallback chain rather than treating the provider call as a single point of failure with no recovery path. The first layer is retrying the same provider with exponential backoff for what look like transient errors (timeouts, rate limits), since many failures resolve within seconds and a naive immediate-fail approach wastes that recovery window.

For a sustained outage, I would fall back to a secondary provider or a different model tier that can serve the same request type, which requires maintaining prompts and integration code that work across at least two providers in advance, not scrambling to build that integration during an actual incident. I would accept that the fallback model might be somewhat lower quality or higher cost, and treat that as a deliberate, monitored trade-off during a degraded-mode window, not a silent quality regression nobody notices.

If both the primary and fallback providers are unavailable, or for requests where a lower-quality answer would be actively harmful, I would return a clear, honest degraded-service message rather than a generic error, and where feasible serve a cached response for common queries as a last resort rather than nothing at all.

I would monitor and alert on which path is actually being used in real time (primary, fallback, degraded) so the team has visibility the moment a provider issue starts, rather than finding out from user complaints, and I'd run periodic fire-drills that simulate a primary-provider failure to confirm the fallback path actually works before we need it for real.
hints: Build a defined fallback chain: retry with backoff, then a secondary provider/model, then a graceful degraded response.
Maintain and test cross-provider integration in advance, not during an actual incident.
Monitor which path is active in real time and run periodic fire-drills simulating a provider outage.

blocks.title: Simple practical implementation
blocks.explanation: The chain tries the primary provider with backoff for transient errors first, falls back to a pre-integrated secondary provider if the primary is truly unavailable, and only returns a clear degraded message as the last resort, so a provider outage degrades the experience instead of breaking it entirely.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.mistake: Calling a single model provider directly with no retry, no fallback provider, and no degraded-mode response, treating a provider API call like a reliable internal function call.
blocks.whyItHappens: During development, a single provider's API works reliably enough that the failure path never gets exercised, so it's easy to underestimate how often transient errors, rate limits and occasional outages occur at real production scale over time, until an actual incident makes the gap obvious.
blocks.correctApproach: Build a defined fallback chain (retry with backoff, then a secondary provider or model tier, then a graceful degraded response) and pre-integrate and test the fallback path before it's needed in a real incident, not during one.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and validation
blocks.content: Routing and fallback both add real engineering complexity, maintaining multiple model integrations, classification logic, and monitoring, so the investment should scale with actual traffic volume and the real cost of an outage or wasted spend, not be built out to maximal sophistication on day one.
keyPoints: Maintain and periodically test a working integration with at least one fallback provider or model tier before an incident forces you to build it live.
Validate routing decisions against an eval set per difficulty tier, not just intuition about which requests are 'simple'.
Monitor and alert on which path (primary, fallback, degraded) is active in real time, not just on aggregate error rates.

blocks.title: Likely follow-up
blocks.question: How would you decide the difficulty classifier used for routing without it becoming another unreliable point of failure?
blocks.answer: Keep the classifier itself cheap, fast and simple, favoring heuristics or a small model over another complex system, and add a mid-request escalation path where a low-confidence response from the cheaper model triggers an automatic retry against the stronger model, so a wrong routing decision degrades to extra cost or latency rather than a wrong answer reaching the user.
